records.claim: the coordinate of the target is approximated by the average location of the K closest RPs in the fingerprint database
records.quote: In KNN, the coordinate of the target is approximated by the average location of the K K closest RPs in the fingerprint database.

records.claim: the locations of the K closest neighbors are given different weights before averaging them
records.quote: In Weighted KNN (WKNN) the locations of the K K closest neighbors are given different weights before averaging them

records.claim: using fixed K might result in large localization estimation errors due to RSS variations or the placement of the RPs
records.conditions: due to RSS variations or the placement of the RPs
records.quote: The standard KNN uses fixed K K value; however, due to RSS variations or the placement of the RPs (e.g., enforced by the environment structure), using fixed K K might result in large localization estimation errors.

records.claim: groups the K nearest RP neighbors in different clusters (according to their locations), then the final location is the average of the RPs in the ”delegate” cluster
records.quote: For instance, the solution in [ 318 ] groups the K K nearest RP neighbors in different clusters (according to their locations), then the final location is the average of the RPs in the ”delegate” cluster.

records.claim: suggests using both the Euclidean distance and the cosine similarity between the RSSI values as a similarity metric, which they also use to construct the weights for a WKNN
records.quote: The work in [ 287 ] suggests using both the Euclidean distance and the cosine similarity between the RSSI values as a similarity metric, which they also use to construct the weights for a WKNN.

records.claim: built a cascaded localization system based on KNN, where a KNN is used to first identify the environment, then for localization they apply KNN with different features (RSSI, the CFR and its auto-correlation function)
records.quote: In [ 296 ] the authors built a cascaded localization system based on KNN, where a KNN is used to first identify the environment, then for localization they apply KNN with different features (RSSI, the CFR and its auto-correlation function).

records.claim: uses AoA to sub-select a group of the K RPs that satisfy an AoA constraint
records.conditions: in MIMO system
records.quote: for instance [ 303 ] uses AoA to sub-select a group of the K K RPs that satisfy an AoA constraint.

records.claim: localization is performed by applying a WKNN to the K nearest fingerprints, where the weights are functions of the proposed metric that correspond to the AoA and ToA
records.conditions: fingerprint-based single-site localization method for massive-MIMO OFDM systems
records.quote: Finally, localization is performed by applying a WKNN to the K nearest fingerprints, where the weights are functions of the proposed metric that correspond to the AoA and ToA.

records.claim: localization is obtained from a WKNN based on the minimum Euclidean distance of the features
records.conditions: construct the database of the angle-delay domain representation by compressing the database and applying a fast method to retrieve the candidate RPs using hashing algorithms
records.quote: localization is obtained from a WKNN based on the minimum Euclidean distance of the features.

records.claim: fingerprint based localization uses KNN over RSS from WiFi, which is used as a coarse estimate of the location to speed up the search space of images based localization
records.conditions: crowd-sourcing indoor localization algorithm via an optical camera and orientation sensor on a smartphone
records.quote: In this solution fingerprint based localization uses KNN over RSS from WiFi, which is used as a coarse estimate of the location to speed up the search space of images based localization

records.claim: many advanced ML solutions use it as a final step to predict the location, where different methods are proposed to define the ”distance” between the fingerprints and the weights
records.quote: In summary, since WKNN is an intuitive technique, many advanced ML solutions use it as a final step to predict the location, where different methods are proposed to define the ”distance” between the fingerprints and the weights.

records.claim: aims at finding the best hyperplane to separate different classes
records.quote: One of the powerful algorithms that uses kernels is the Support Vector Machine (SVM). It aims at finding the best hyperplane to separate different classes.

records.claim: allows SVM to use the kernels to find efficiently this product in higher (possibly infinite) dimensional space, which can increase the separability of the features
records.conditions: predictions usually appear in the form of inner products between training instances and observed feature
records.quote: this allows SVM to use the kernels to find efficiently this product in higher (possibly infinite) dimensional space, which can increase the separability of the features

records.claim: uses SVM for localization in a WSN that has a few sensors with known locations
records.conditions: sensors measure the RSSI between one another
records.quote: In one of the early works that uses kernel based localization, [ 78 ] uses SVM for localization in a WSN that has a few sensors with known locations.

records.claim: uses linear and Gaussian kernels for room level localization using cellular RSSI
records.quote: Ref. [ 76 ] uses linear and Gaussian kernels for room level localization using cellular RSSI.

records.claim: localizes the target using SVM with an RBF kernel after reducing dimensionality of RSSI features through PCA
records.conditions: first reduces the dimensionality of the RSSI features through PCA
records.quote: Ref. [ 249 ] first reduces the dimensionality of the RSSI features through PCA, then localizes the target using SVM with an RBF kernel.

records.claim: use SVM to classify the target location after sorting RSSIs from the most reliable APs
records.conditions: address the diversity of the devices
records.quote: In [ 104 ] the authors propose a method to address the diversity of the devices by first sorting the RSSIs from the most reliable APs, then use SVM to classify the target location.

records.claim: used ToA and RSSI in Gaussian kernel Ridge regression for localization
records.quote: In [ 165 ] the authors used ToA and RSSI in Gaussian kernel Ridge regression for localization.

records.claim: uses TOA as fingerprints, and proposes a Gaussian Kernel based solution; the proposed approach is insensitive to random synchronization and measurement timing errors
records.quote: Ref. [ 203 ] uses TOA as fingerprints, and proposes a Gaussian Kernel based solution; the proposed approach is insensitive to random synchronization and measurement timing errors.

records.claim: features are then fed to an SVM algorithm for hierarchical region classification
records.conditions: extracting different features from the channel impulse response, such as the energy decay time
records.quote: The features are then fed to an SVM algorithm for hierarchical region classification.

records.claim: constructed a visibility graph that captures the frequency correlations between adjacent sub-carriers, which are used for localization with SVM
records.conditions: Using CSI of 30 sub-carriers
records.quote: Using CSI of 30 sub-carriers, [ 60 ] constructed a visibility graph that captures the frequency correlations between adjacent sub-carriers, which are used for localization with SVM.

records.claim: the SVM is first used to classify the target in one of the possible activity classes, then the localization is done with the associated localization regression model
records.conditions: CSI based activity recognition and localization
records.quote: CSI based activity recognition and localization using SVM and kernel regression is proposed in [ 229 ] , where the SVM is first used to classify the target in one of the possible activity classes, then the localization is done with the associated localization regression model.

records.claim: SVM for ranging error estimation based on CSI in an UWB system
records.quote: Kernel methods have been used in other aspects of localization, such as an SVM for ranging error estimation based on CSI in an UWB system in [ 224 ]

records.claim: uses SVR to reconstruct the RSSI values of the non-selected APs
records.conditions: proposes a solution for AP selection and classification
records.quote: To improve the robustness of the localization process against noise, [ 182 ] proposes a solution for AP selection and classification, then uses SVR to reconstruct the RSSI values of the non-selected APs.

records.claim: suggests using kernel canonical correlation analysis to better capture the correlation in the signal (RSSI) space and the coordinates before the localization
records.conditions: Gaussian and Matern kernels are used for signal space and physical space, respectively
records.quote: Ref. [ 324 ] suggests using kernel canonical correlation analysis to better capture the correlation in the signal (RSSI) space and the coordinates before the localization, where Gaussian and Matern kernels are used for signal space and physical space, respectively.

records.claim: propose using a sum-of-exponentials kernel that is tolerant to missing values and sensitive to feature differences in RSSI based cellular positioning
records.quote: In [ 325 ] the authors propose using a sum-of-exponentials kernel that is tolerant to missing values and sensitive to feature differences in RSSI based cellular positioning.

records.claim: an Import Vector Machine (IVM) was used for NLOS classification for ToA based ranging in UWB systems; the authors point out that ISM has less complexity and represents better classification probability
records.quote: In [ 80 ] an Import Vector Machine (IVM) was used for NLOS classification for ToA based ranging in UWB systems; the authors point out that ISM has less complexity and represents better classification probability.

records.claim: propose to use GP regression on the training data to build a continuous distribution of the RSSI for each AP
records.quote: In [ 326 ] the authors propose to use GP regression on the training data to build a continuous distribution of the RSSI for each AP.

records.claim: uses a GP to model the probability distribution of the RSSI values, then for a given RSSI observation, and using Bayes rule, the location is estimated by a weighted combination of the RPs’ locations
records.quote: Ref. [ 328 ] uses a GP to model the probability distribution of the RSSI values, then for a given RSSI observation, and using Bayes rule, the location is estimated by a weighted combination of the RPs’ locations.

records.claim: describes a method for dynamically estimating and calibrating the RSSI radio map using GP; for this the standard deviation of the trained GP model is used to measure the accuracy of the estimated position; the final location is estimated using WKNN
records.quote: Ref. [ 329 ] describes a method for dynamically estimating and calibrating the RSSI radio map using GP; for this the standard deviation of the trained GP model is used to measure the accuracy of the estimated position; the final location is estimated using WKNN.

records.claim: introduce numerical approximation GP methods that result in a test Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) very close to the Cramér–Rao bound, which is verified with simulated data
records.conditions: For a distributed massive-MIMO system
records.quote: For a distributed massive-MIMO system, [ 113 ] introduce numerical approximation GP methods that result in a test Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) very close to the Cramér–Rao bound, which is verified with simulated data.

records.claim: a subset of these projections is then used as an input for GPR to provide a ranging estimate
records.conditions: using a kernel PCA, in which the selected channel parameters are projected onto a nonlinear orthogonal high-dimensional space
records.quote: The first step consists of using a kernel PCA, in which the selected channel parameters are projected onto a nonlinear orthogonal high-dimensional space; a subset of these projections is then used as an input for GPR to provide a ranging estimate.

records.claim: applies Volume Cross-Correlation on the CSI to acquire the TDOA, then uses a RaF for classification-based localization using multi-path information
records.conditions: The proposed solution uses a combination of both ray-tracing and measurements to enhance the localization performance.
records.quote: For example, [ 204 ] applies Volume Cross-Correlation on the CSI to acquire the TDOA, then uses a RaF for classification-based localization using multi-path information.

records.claim: uses the RSSI in WiFi networks to provide the location in terms of both coordinates and room-level prediction
records.conditions: In the offline phase, fingerprint data are pre-processed, ensemble classifiers (based on GMM) are trained for room prediction, and a RaF regressor is trained for location prediction.
records.quote: Ref. [ 53 ] uses the RSSI in WiFi networks to provide the location in terms of both coordinates and room-level prediction.

records.claim: utilizes a multi-antenna system to build fingerprints with different features, such as RSSI, power spectral density, and other statistical features
records.conditions: For each feature a RaF is trained as classifier.
records.quote: Ref. [ 79 ] utilizes a multi-antenna system to build fingerprints with different features, such as RSSI, power spectral density, and other statistical features.

records.claim: proposes a ﬁngerprinting method by transforming raw RSSI into features with a learned non-linear mapping function using GBRF
records.conditions: Due to fluctuation of the RSSI signals, the RSSI distance might not reflect the true location distance
records.quote: to address this [ 142 ] proposes a ﬁngerprinting method by transforming raw RSSI into features with a learned non-linear mapping function using GBRF.

records.claim: employs Adaboost for passive localization, where the phase information in CSI is used to construct the ﬁngerprint map
records.conditions: Through continuous iteration with the Adaboost algorithm, the sample weights of the training sets are continuously adjusted to prepare for classiﬁcation.
records.quote: Ref. [ 57 ] employs Adaboost for passive localization, where the phase information in CSI is used to construct the ﬁngerprint map.

records.claim: compares KNN, RaF and SVM for device-free localization using CSI
records.quote: Ref. [ 237 ] compares KNN, RaF and SVM for device-free localization using CSI.

records.claim: suggests localization using frequency modulation and digital video broadcasting terrestrial signals, comparing KNN and, SVM and SVM with Ensemble Learning
records.quote: Ref. [ 129 ] suggests localization using frequency modulation and digital video broadcasting terrestrial signals, comparing KNN and, SVM and SVM with Ensemble Learning.

records.claim: uses the RSRP of the three strongest BSs along with their locations in an LTE network as input to localize the user
records.quote: Ref. [ 247 ] uses the RSRP of the three strongest BSs along with their locations in an LTE network as input to localize the user.

records.claim: uses an NN, with three hidden layers, that takes RSSI from a number of BSs; data augmentation techniques improve robustness
records.quote: Ref. [ 192 ] uses an NN, with three hidden layers, that takes RSSI from a number of BSs. Data augmentation techniques, e.g., masking some of the BS values, improve the robustness of the solution.

records.claim: trains two networks for TOA and RSSI from WiFi; location is a weighted combination of outputs
records.quote: In [ 250 ] , two networks are trained for two different features, namely TOA and RSSI from a WiFi systems, and the location is a weighted combination of the outputs of the two networks.

records.claim: uses a hierarchical localization solution where an NN is trained for each indoor location; online phase identifies environment then passes RSSI to corresponding NN
records.quote: Ref. [ 151 ] uses a hierarchical localization solution, where for each indoor location, an NN is trained. During the online phase, the real-time RSSI measurements (from WiFi or/and cellular) are first used to identify the environment, and then they are passed as input to the corresponding trained NN.

records.claim: builds fingerprints using RSSI (or CSI amplitude) with directional antennas; uses NN with two hidden layers as classifier; rough AoA estimate improves accuracy
records.conditions: Using directional antennas in a WiFi system
records.quote: Using directional antennas in a WiFi system, [ 206 ] builds fingerprints using RSSI (or CSI amplitude) and uses an NN with two hidden layers as a classifier to predict the closest fingerprint to the observed values. Using a rough estimate of the AoA provides an improved localization accuracy.

records.claim: uses CSI amplitude at 16 antennas and 924 sub-carriers as input to several NNs (ensemble); final location is combination of outputs; median and weighted average method provided best result
records.conditions: For an 8 × 2 MIMO system
records.quote: For an 8 × 2 MIMO system, [ 238 ] uses CSI amplitude at 16 antennas and 924 sub-carriers as input to several NNs with different hyperparameters (i.e., an ensemble learning solution); the final location is a combination of the output from all networks. This paper also studied different combining techniques; a method that uses both the median and weighted average of the location estimates provided the best result.

records.claim: is a simplified feed-forward NN architecture with one hidden layer; first layer weights are random, hidden layer weights calculated with least square fit
records.quote: Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) is a simplified feed-forward NN architecture with one hidden layer. The weights of the first layer are set to random values, while the weights for the hidden layer are usually calculated with the least square fit.

records.claim: creates WiFi RSSI fingerprint database offline and trains ELM; online phase updates solution with new fingerprints and uses latest ELM to predict coordinates
records.quote: In [ 159 ] , during the offline phase, a WiFi RSSI fingerprint database is created, and an ELM is trained on the data. During the online phase, fingerprints are still collected at some known locations, and the solution is updated according to the new fingerprints too. Then the latest ELM is used to predict the coordinates.

records.claim: clusters data using k-means offline; uses ELM to classify data to clusters and trains dedicated ELM for each; online phase classifies RSSI then uses associated cluster ELM
records.quote: In Ref. [ 173 ] , during the offline phase, the data is first clustered using k-means clustering, an ELM is used to classify the data to one of the clusters, and a dedicated ELM for each cluster is trained. During the online phase, the RSSI values are first classified and then the ELM of the associated cluster is used.

records.claim: introduces framework for target tracking using RSSI from WiFi, Bluetooth, XBee and yaw readings; uses Gaussian Outliers Filtering and particle filter
records.quote: A framework that utilizes features from different technologies for target tracking was introduced in [ 111 ] . The inputs to the NN are: the RSSI measurements from WiFi, Bluetooth and XBee (a wireless connectivity module used for IoT) from different nodes, plus yaw readings when available. The yaw readings can be extracted by filtering measurements of some wearable sensors (accelerometer, magnetometer and gyroscope). The probabilities of fingerprints are passed through a Gaussian Outliers Filtering process, and the output can then be weighted and combined to provide the location estimate, which in turn is fed to a particle filter for target tracking.

records.claim: proposes fingerprint-based localization scheme utilizing magnitude of CSI at 90 sub-carriers from three antennas; uses weights of NNs with four hidden layers as fingerprints; trained by greedy learning with stack of RBMs
records.conditions: For MIMO-OFDM systems
records.quote: For MIMO-OFDM systems, [ 297 ] proposes a fingerprint-based localization scheme (which is called DeepFi) that utilizes the magnitude of the CSI at 90 sub-carriers from three antennas. It uses the weights of NNs with four hidden layers to represent the fingerprints. Training the NNs is done by a greedy learning algorithm using a stack of RBMs (see sec. II-A ).

records.claim: online phase uses Gaussian RBF kernel to represent likelihood probability; Bayes rule calculates posterior probability; final location is weighted average of RP locations
records.quote: During the online phase, using a number of RSSI realizations (packets), a Gaussian RBF kernel is used to represent the likelihood probability of the observed data when i th i^{\rm th} location (RP) is true, from which Bayes rule can be used to calculate the posterior probability of location i i . The final location is the weighted average of all RP locations.

records.claim: proposes scheme utilizing phase value to construct fingerprint database; linear transformation of phase value improves stability; weights of three-hidden-layer-NNs serve as fingerprints
records.quote: Ref. [ 331 ] proposes a scheme (called PhaseFi) that utilizes the phase value to construct a fingerprint database, where a linear transformation of the phase value as a calibration step, improves the stability of the phase values. The weights of a three-hidden-layer-NNs serve as fingerprints.

records.claim: considers NNs in passive localization using amplitude and calibrated phase of CSI as hybrid complex input feature to detect human presence
records.quote: NNs in passive localization have been considered in [ 58 ] , where amplitude and the calibrated phase of CSI are used as a hybrid complex input feature to the NN to detect the presence of a human.

records.claim: integrates NNs in a cooperative WLS estimator in mmWave communication systems
records.conditions: In mmWave communication systems
records.quote: In mmWave communication systems, [ 183 ] integrates NNs in a cooperative WLS estimator.

records.claim: uses RSSI values as input to an NN to predict ranging error; localization algorithm uses adjusted range values
records.quote: NNs were used for ranging error mitigation in [ 201 ] , where the authors use RSSI values as input to an NN, which then predicts the ranging error; a localization algorithm such as least squares can then use the adjusted range values.

records.claim: uses a CNN applied to RSSI image to classify location in one of several buildings and floor levels
records.quote: Ref. [ 281 ] uses a CNN, applied to the RSSI image, to classify the location in one of several buildings and floor levels.

records.claim: augments features with correlation values; uses augmented image in hierarchical structure: CNN predicts floor, then corridor, then coordinates
records.quote: Ref. [ 316 ] augments the features with correlation values (between the RSSI from the AP at all RPs and their locations). The augmented image is used as input to a hierarchical localization structure, where initially a CNN predicts the floor number, then a CNN associated with the chosen floor predicts the corridor number, and finally a CNN associated with that corridor is used to estimate the coordinates.

records.claim: proposes hybrid RSSI features containing ratio of contribution of RSSI value to fingerprint
records.quote: Ref. [ 105 ] proposes hybrid RSSI features that contain the ratio of the contribution of the RSSI value to the fingerprint.

records.claim: uses CWT to produce 2D time-frequency image from RSSI time series; CNN predicts closest reference points; KNN infers coordinates
records.quote: Viewing the RSSI values as time series, Ref. [ 307 ] uses CWT (see Sec. IV ) to produce a 2D time-frequency image; the CNN predicts the closest reference points to the target, and KNN is then used to infer the coordinates of the target.

records.claim: uses RSSI values from all APs over different time instances to form RSSI-time 2D images to predict building, floor and coordinates
records.quote: In another hierarchical localization model, [ 256 ] uses RSSI values from all APs over different time instances to form RSSI-time 2D images to predict the building, floor and coordinates.

records.claim: uses BLE RSSI observations over time for vehicle and pedestrian detection/localization in a smart parking system
records.quote: BLE RSSI observations over time are used in [ 286 ] for vehicle and pedestrian detection/localization in a smart parking system.

records.claim: uses RSSI values from several APs to predict location with two capsule networks, one for 2.4 GHz and one for 5 GHz
records.quote: In [ 227 ] , the RSSI values from several APs are used to predict the location with two capsule networks, one for the RSSI values in 2.4 2.4 GHz and one for RSSI values in 5 5 GHz.

records.claim: is a multi-layer CNN network that uses amplitudes of the CFR at the available sub-carriers (in a WiFi system) at a number of time instances to form an image; realizations at different antennas can be used at different CNN channels, and the output is the probability that a target is located at a given RP
records.quote: The ”ConFi” scheme [ 333 ] is a multi-layer CNN network that uses amplitudes of the CFR at the available sub-carriers (in a WiFi system) at a number of time instances to form an image; realizations at different antennas can be used at different CNN channels (see Sec. II-A ), and the output is the probability that a target is located at a given RP, see Fig. 5 .

records.claim: The final location is estimated by averaging the location of the RPs with their predicted probabilities.
records.quote: The final location is estimated by averaging the location of the RPs with their predicted probabilities.

records.claim: uses coarse but stable estimates of the AoA, based on the pair-wise phase difference between antennas. The provided example uses the 30 available sub-carriers and 960 time instances to form 16 60 × 60 images for training. During the online phase it predicts the location by fusing the location of the most probable reference points.
records.quote: The so-called ”CiFi” scheme [ 205 ] uses coarse but stable estimates of the AoA, based on the pair-wise phase difference between antennas. The provided example uses the 30 available sub-carriers and 960 time instances to form 16 60 × 60 images for training. During the online phase it predicts the location by fusing the location of the most probable reference points.

records.claim: uses the learned spatio-temporal features through dual stream 3D CNNs to approximate the posterior distribution of the mobile device’s location with a GMM. It creates two 3D images of the calibrated phase and amplitude of the CSI, where the height, the width, and the depth (number of channels) are, respectively, the amplitude/phase from different packets, different sub-carriers (30 available) and Tx-Rx antenna combinations.
records.quote: Ref. [ 242 ] uses the learned spatio-temporal features through dual stream 3D CNNs to approximate the posterior distribution of the mobile device’s location with a GMM. It creates two 3D images of the calibrated phase and amplitude of the CSI, where the height, the width, and the depth (number of channels) are, respectively, the amplitude/phase from different packets, different sub-carriers (30 available) and Tx-Rx antenna combinations.

records.claim: creates three-channel images that have the amplitudes of all sub-carrier × packet samples in one channel, and pair-wise phase differences between the antenna signals in the two other channels. They use ShuffleNet, a computationally efficient deep CNN architecture, to predict the most probable RPs.
records.conditions: In a three-antenna system
records.quote: In a three-antenna system, [ 232 ] creates three-channel images that have the amplitudes of all sub-carrier × packet samples in one channel, and pair-wise phase differences between the antenna signals in the two other channels. They use ShuffleNet, a computationally efficient deep CNN architecture, to predict the most probable RPs.

records.claim: proposes 3D images that have power values in horizontal, vertical, and delay domains. The images are fed to a CNN network that uses the inception module and different kernel sizes (due to different sparsity at different domains).
records.conditions: For a Uniform Planar Array
records.quote: For a Uniform Planar Array, [ 212 ] proposes 3D images that have power values in horizontal, vertical, and delay domains. The images are fed to a CNN network that uses the inception module and different kernel sizes (due to different sparsity at different domains).

records.claim: creates images using the time sequence of RSSI values and their CWT; the solution then detects the presence of users indoor.
records.quote: For instance, [ 271 ] creates images using the time sequence of RSSI values and their CWT; the solution then detects the presence of users indoor.

records.claim: the authors use 1D CNN networks with either RSSI values from all antennas over several packets or CSI amplitudes from all sub-carries and antennas. They notice the superior performance of CSI based solutions to detect the region of the target.
records.quote: In [ 233 ] , the authors use 1D CNN networks with either RSSI values from all antennas over several packets or CSI amplitudes from all sub-carries and antennas. They notice the superior performance of CSI based solutions to detect the region of the target.

records.claim: uses a CNN network for ranging error mitigation, proposing two approaches,: one for NLOS detection and another one to estimate the ranging error.
records.conditions: For ranging in UWB systems
records.quote: For ranging in UWB systems, Ref. [ 225 ] uses a CNN network for ranging error mitigation, proposing two approaches,: one for NLOS detection and another one to estimate the ranging error.

records.claim: proposes to use time-calibrated complex CIRs to create images. The authors modified several of popular deep networks such as AlexNet and GoogLeNet. They found that GoogLeNet gives a good complexity-to-performance trade-off. They also propose a distributed framework to reduce the overhead.
records.conditions: In an industrial environment, where ranging based on ToA is difficult, due to the increased multi-path propagation
records.quote: In an industrial environment, where ranging based on ToA is difficult, due to the increased multi-path propagation, Ref. [ 240 ] proposes to use time-calibrated complex CIRs to create images. The authors modified several of popular deep networks such as AlexNet and GoogLeNet. They found that GoogLeNet gives a good complexity-to-performance trade-off. They also propose a distributed framework to reduce the overhead.

records.claim: uses a sequence of RSSI values as input to cascaded RNNs to estimate both the building and the floor numbers.
records.quote: Ref. [ 334 ] uses a sequence of RSSI values as input to cascaded RNNs to estimate both the building and the floor numbers.

records.claim: proposes efficient construction of the fingerprint database for real-time systems with RSSI samples, where LSTM is used for localization.
records.conditions: In a system with multiple BLE anchors
records.quote: In a system with multiple BLE anchors, [ 284 ] proposes efficient construction of the fingerprint database for real-time systems with RSSI samples, where LSTM is used for localization.

records.claim: use the RSSI history from only the associated cell tower to track users’ location with an LSTM, where the inputs are (cell tower ID, RSS) sequential pairs and the output is the 2D coordinates.
records.conditions: In a cellular system
records.quote: In a cellular system, Refs. [ 115 , 283 ] use the RSSI history from only the associated cell tower to track users’ location with an LSTM, where the inputs are (cell tower ID, RSS) sequential pairs and the output is the 2D coordinates.

records.claim: proposes using KNN and HMM to generate synthetic measurements based on the previously observed ones.
records.conditions: To train the LSTM
records.quote: To train the LSTM, Ref. [ 283 ] proposes using KNN and HMM to generate synthetic measurements based on the previously observed ones.

records.claim: the authors apply a sliding window to the sequence of RSSI samples; in each window they calculate five features (minimum, maximum, and three quartile values) from each AP. They then feed them as a sequence of vectors to an LSTM
records.quote: In [ 272 ] , the authors apply a sliding window to the sequence of RSSI samples; in each window they calculate five features (minimum, maximum, and three quartile values) from each AP. They then feed them as a sequence of vectors to an LSTM, see Fig. 6 for more details.

records.claim: uses RSSI values from cellular and WiFi systems, the solution takes the RSSI fingerprint from multiple APs/BSs at multiple timesteps and passes them to a single-layer RNN which then gives the coordinates.
records.conditions: In cellular and WiFi systems
records.quote: In cellular and WiFi systems, [ 149 ] uses RSSI values from cellular and WiFi systems, the solution takes the RSSI fingerprint from multiple APs/BSs at multiple timesteps and passes them to a single-layer RNN which then gives the coordinates.

records.claim: proposes using RSSI from three UAV-BSs and nearby WiFi APs to predict the location. records.subject: Counterfactual explanations

claims.claim: Mincu et al. (2021) presents a system that can be a tool for medical experts to create counterfactual explanations.
The system helps understand consequences of alternative historical decisions, such as different antibiotic types affecting recovery speed.

records.quote: The same holds for the proof of concept in Mincu et al. (2021) where a system in the hands of a person holding medical expertise can be a tool useful to create counterfactual explanations. The explanans presented by the system, together with other explanantia, can open up to better understand the consequences of an alternative historical decision. For example that it is probable that using a different type of antibiotics on women than men will make women recover faster.

records.subject: Kind-data explanation

claims.claim: In Lucieri et al. (2020), similar images and the trained model create the explanans for identifying skin lesions.
The explanation answers if an instance belongs to a concept quality by presenting similar images as evidence.

records.quote: For example, in Lucieri et al. (2020) , that focuses on identifying skin lesions, the images presented as similar to the image to be explained, together, with the trained model create the explanans that are a selected part of the available explanandum. This explanandum then answers a question of the form: This instance belongs to the concept quality a (a specific skin lesion concept) presenting these similar images as evidence/explanans for the decision ( quality b ).

records.subject: Contrastive explanation

claims.claim: Chen et al. (2020) uses a proof of concept experiment with disentangled kind and sub-kind concepts.
A contrastive explanation is formulated around the model's inner workings, e.g., classifying as BEDROOM not STABLE due to PERSON and BED sub-kinds.
The explanation is not causal in a real-world context but gives insights into how the model associates input with outputs.

records.quote: In one example by Chen et al. (2020) the correlation between five disentangled kind concepts: BEDROOM, AIRFIELD, STABLE, BOAT DECK and INDOOR LIBRARY and seven disentangled sub- kind concepts: AEROPLANE, BED, BENCH, BOAT, BOOK, HORSE, PERSON is part of a proof of concept experiment. Here the explanadum consists of the classified kind , the trained model and sub- kinds pictured and not pictured in the image. A contrastive explanation can then be formulated around the inner workings of the model for example that: since the sub- kinds identified are PERSON and BED the model classifies the picture as a BEDROOM and not a STABLE . This explanation is contrastive from the trained model’s perspective in the sense that it explains the classification and that it is likely that images containing a bed and a person will be classified as bedrooms. Here, again, knowledge priors in the form of selection of kinds and sub- kinds , but also training data and model selection, together delimits the explanadum available. So even if the form of the explanation can be classified as intervention the explanation is not causal in the sense that it holds in a real world context, instead it gives insights in how the trained model associate input data with outputs.

records.subject: structured models

claims.claim: Hybrid structures are the combination of different sub-models to a single structured model, divided into Parallel, Series, and Parameter scheduling models.
Projection-based structures project the input space into a lower-dimensional latent space.
Additive structures group input dimensions into sub-spaces acting as input to sub-models, with the output being the sum of sub-models' outputs.
Hierarchical structures are composed of parallel, series, and additive structures yielding hierarchical causal relationships.
Input space decompositions decompose the input space into regions that constitute a sub-space to a sub-model, split region-wise rather than dimension-wise.

records.quote: Hybrid structures : The combination of different sub-models to a single structured model. ... Parallel model : The outputs of all sub-models are summed up... Series model : The sub-models are connected in series... Parameter scheduling model : The parameters of a sub-model are scheduled... Projection-based structures : The input space is projected into a lower-dimensional latent space. Additive structures : The input dimensions are grouped into several sub-spaces... Hierarchical structures : A model is composed of parallel, series, and additive structures... Input space decompositions : The input space is decomposed into several regions...

records.subject: Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation

claims.claim: Transfer learning in MS lesion segmentation includes using pre-trained models from other domains and applying trained models on different MS datasets.
Applying trained models on different MS datasets is considered domain adaptation where the target task remains the same but domains differ.
claims.conditions: target task remains the same as the source (i.e., MS lesion segmentation) but the domains (i.e., MRI protocols and therefore image appearance) are different

claims.claim: Multi-task training is also a form of transfer learning.

records.quote: Transfer learning is an active topic in deep learning, and in the context of MS lesion segmentation, it includes two aspects: 1) using pre-trained models from other domains; 2) applying trained model on different MS datasets (e.g., for clinical use). The latter scenario is also considered as domain adaptation, in which the target task remains the same as the source (i.e., MS lesion segmentation) but the domains (i.e., MRI protocols and therefore image appearance) are different. Multi-task training (Sec. 2.4 ) is also a form of transfer learning.

records.subject: event detection work done in ECG event detection

claims.claim: A three states Markov chain was used to model R-R interval sequences to characterize rhythms through probability of observed sequences generated by arrhythmia models.
A parallel combination of HMMs (one for each arrhythmia type) is used to classify arrhythmia by determining the most likely path through the parallel models.
An HMM was constructed for ECG beat with each waveform part represented in the model, with parameters estimated using Baum-Welch method.
An HMM is used for frequency tracking to overcome corruption of residual ECG by muscular activity or insufficient beat cancellation.
An ECG channel along with a phonocardiogram were fused in a single coupled HMM for beat detection, introducing decision-level fusion.
An Elman-based RNN is used for beat classification with the Levenberg-Marquardat algorithm for training, using power spectral density of ECG signals as input.
An LSTM-based RNN preceded by a density-based clustering for training data selection was used for supraventricular and ventricular ectopic beat detection.
A 3 layer RNN was implemented to extract the temporal features from the raw ECG signals for atrial fibrillation automatic detection.
A combination of GRU and bidirectional LSTM (BLSTM) based RNNs and nonparameteric Hidden Semi-Markov Models (HSMM) was used for building the beat classification model.
A single layer LSTM-based convolutional RNN (CRNN) was constructed for atrial fibrillation detection in arbitrary length ECG recordings using log spectrogram as input.
A two layer LSTM-based CRNN was used for atrial fibrillation detection from single-lead ECG and heart rate with feature-level fusion after CNN layers.
A single layer LSTM-based RNN was constructed for atrial fibrillation detection in multi-lead ECG using spectrograms of the input ECG signals.
A deep single-layer LSTM based CRNN was used for classifying ECG beats from single-lead ECG for myocardial infarction classification.

records.subject: log parsing solutions

claims.claim: Existing log parsing solutions are categorized into four categories: clustering-based approaches, frequent pattern mining-based approaches, heuristic approaches, and program analysis.

Program analysis is a code-driven approach that primarily relies on the source code or the compiled executables to associate each log entry to the corresponding log printing statement, while solutions belonging to the other categories are data-driven.

records.quote: Based on our literature review, we categorize existing log parsing solutions into four categories: clustering-based approaches, frequent pattern mining-based approaches, heuristic approaches, and program analysis. Program analysis is a code-driven approach that primarily relies on the source code or the compiled executables to associate each log entry to the corresponding log printing statement, while solutions belonging to the other categories are data-driven.
records.section: III Log parsing solutions: A taxonomy

records.subject: clustering-based log parsing

claims.claim: Existing log parsers employ four clustering algorithms: hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, online clustering, and other clustering methods.

records.quote: For each generated cluster, it employs a merging algorithm, which aligns and merges all the constituent patterns sequentially to generate a new pattern as a log template.

records.subject: LCS-based approach

records.subject: Diversity Metrics

claims.claim: Diversity metrics are categorized into Relevance-oblivious and Relevance-aware classes based on whether item relevance is considered.

Relevance-oblivious metrics include Distance-based (Cosine, Jaccard, Gower), Coverage-based (Rank-unaware: P, C, S, E-Coverage; Rank-aware: S-RR@100%, S-Recall@K, S-Precision@K), and Social Welfare (SD Index, Gini Index).
Relevance-aware metrics include Novelty-based (α-nDCG@K, NRBP, nDCU@K) and IA-family (M-IA, D-family: D-M, D#-M).

records.subject: Individual vs. Joint

(2021b) , and joint retrievers must establish the linking themselves. This could introduce incorrect information and result in a cascade of errors. records.subject: Cell-Based vs. Row-Based vs. Table-Based

claims.claim: Cell-based retrievers can overlook a large amount of useless data but are unable to simulate cross-row or cross-column information of the table structure.
Row-based retriever can better represent the row relation than the cell-based one, but it is still challenging to model the information about the column structure.
Table-based retriever is the only option to manage massive amounts of table data because it is difficult to divide each table into cells or rows.

records.quote: Since HybridQA answers frequently incorporate information from single or multiple cells, cell-based retrievers can overlook a large amount of useless data. However, they are unable to simulate the cross-row or cross-column information of the table structure. The row-based retriever can better represent the row relation than the cell-based one, but it is still challenging to model the information about the column structure. When there are too many words in a sequence, there will be a lot of useless information, and it will be difficult to add additional important information. The only option to manage massive amounts of table data is to use a table-based retriever because it is difficult to divide each table into cells or rows.

records.subject: Direct Action on Images

claims.claim: These direct prediction approaches are highly effective for real world operation, however they are fairly limited in their potential.

Lastly, these approaches typically rely on some synthetic training data, which must be generated via other 3D-aware methods.

records.quote: In cross-device FedRS, different mobile devices are usually treated as participants [ 23 ] [ 10 ] . The typical application of cross-device FedRS is to build a personal recommendation model for users without collecting their local data. In this way, users can enjoy recommend services while protecting their private information. The number of participants in cross-device FedRS is relatively large and each participant keeps a small amount of data. Considering the limited computation and communication abilities of mobile devices, cross-device FedRS cannot handle very complex training tasks.

records.subject: cross-platform FedRS

claims.claim: In cross-platform FedRS, different data platforms are usually treated as participants who want to collaborate to improve recommendation performance while meeting regulation and privacy constraints.
Compared to cross-device FedRS, the number of participants in cross-platform FedRS is relatively small, and each participant owns relative large amount of data.

records.quote: In cross-platform FedRS, different data platforms are usually treated as participants who want to collaborate to improve recommendation performance while meeting regulation and privacy constraints [ 24 ] [ 25 ] [ 26 ] . For example, to improve the recommendation performance, recommendation systems often integrate data from multiple platforms (e.g., e-commercial platforms, social platforms) [ 27 ] . However, due to privacy and regulation concerns, the different data platforms are often unable to directly share their data with each other. In this scenario, cross-platform FedRS can be used to collaboratively train recommendation models between different data platforms without directly exchanging their users’ data. Compared to cross-device FedRS, the number of participants in cross-platform FedRS is relatively small, and each participant owns relative large amount of data.

records.subject: Heterogeneity of Federated Recommendation Systems

claims.claim: FedRS face more severe challenges in terms of heterogeneity, mainly reflected in system heterogeneity, statistical heterogeneity and model heterogeneity.
System heterogeneity refers to client devices have significantly different storage, computation, and communication capabilities.
Statistical heterogeneity refers to the data collected by different clients is usually not independent and identically distributed (non-IID).
Privacy heterogeneity means that the privacy constraints of different users and information vary greatly.

records.quote: Compared with traditional recommendation systems, FedRS face more severe challenges in terms of heterogeneity, which are mainly reflected in system heterogeneity, statistical heterogeneity and model heterogeneity, as shown in Fig. 3 . System heterogeneity refers to client devices have significantly different storage, computation, and communication capabilities. Devices with limited capabilities greatly affect training efficiency, and further reduce the accuracy of the global recommendation model. [ 61 ] ; Statistical heterogeneity refers to the data collected by different clients is usually not independent and identically distributed (non-IID). As a result, simply training a single global model is difficult to generalize to all clients, which affects the personalization of recommendations [ 62 ] ; Privacy heterogeneity means that the privacy constraints of different users and information vary greatly, so simply treating them with the same privacy budgets will carry unnecessary costs [ 63 ] .

records.claim: The architecture contains an encoder-decoder structure, with the encoder module containing N stacked identical blocks, each having two sub-layers of a multi-head self-attention network and a point-wise fully connected feed-forward network.
records.quote: The architecture of the transformer model contains an encoder-decoder structure, as shown in Figure 14 . The left side of this image shows a simple schematic of the transformer. The encoder module contains N N stacked identical blocks, with each block having two sub-layers of a multi-head self-attention network and a point-wise fully connected feed-forward network.

records.claim: The decoder comprises N identical blocks, each having three sub-layers of multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and feed-forward, where the encoder-decoder attention sublayer performs multi-head attention on the outputs of the corresponding encoder block.
records.quote: The decoder in the transformer model also comprises N N identical blocks. Each decoder block has three sub-layers of multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and feed-forward. The multi-head self-attention and feed-forward are similar to the encoder, while the encoder-decoder attention sublayer performs multi-head attention on the outputs of the corresponding encoder block.

records.subject: Extracting Structures from Source Code

claims.claim: Researchers propose to utilize rich structural information of source code, such as AST, CFGs, and DFGs, extracted in the preprocessing phase for code modeling.
Code structures can be flattened into sequences to be input into Transformers, using attention masks to recover structural information.
An alternative method uses an encoding function to map ASTs into sequences that can be directly input into the transformer without losing structural information.

records.quote: To be specific, it is possible to extract the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Control-Flow Graphs (CFGs), and Data-Flow Graphs (DFGs) in the preprocessing phase and utilize these structures in code modeling Peng et al. (2021b) ; Shiv and Quirk (2019) ; Guo et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2021a) ; Guo et al. (2022) . One common method of flattening code structures is to obtain a sequence of nodes by traversing the graph or tree and using attention masks in the self-attention to recover the structural information, which will be discussed in Section 2.2.2 . An alternative method, proposed by Guo et al. (2022) , is to use an encoding function to map ASTs into sequences that can be directly input into the transformer without losing structural information.

records.subject: MWP datasets

claims.claim: Ape210K consists of 210k elementary math word problems, which is the largest publicly available.
The problems in GSM8K can involve up to 8 steps to solve.
SVAMP is a benchmark that tests the robustness of deep learning models to math word problems with simple variations.
IconQA provides an abstract diagram as a visual context, while TabMWP provides a tabular context for each problem.
MathQA is annotated with precise operation programs, and MathQA-Python is provided with specific Python programs instead.
Lila annotates many of the previously mentioned MWP datasets with Python program rationales.

records.quote: Ape210K Zhao et al. (2020) consists of 210k elementary math word problems, which is the largest publicly available. The problems in GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) can involve up to 8 steps to solve. SVAMP Patel et al. (2021) is a benchmark that tests the robustness of deep learning models to math word problems with simple variations. More recently built datasets involve modalities beyond text. For example, IconQA Lu et al. (2021b) provides an abstract diagram as a visual context, while TabMWP Lu et al. (2022b) provides a tabular context for each problem. Most MWP datasets provide annotated equations as a rationale for the solution (e.g., Table 1 ). To improve the performance and interpretability of the learned solvers, MathQA Tafjord et al. (2019) is annotated with precise operation programs, and MathQA-Python Austin et al. (2021) is provided with specific Python programs instead. Another line of datasets annotates the problems with multi-step natural language solutions that are regarded as more human-readable Ling et al. (2017) ; Cobbe et al. (2021) ; Lu et al. (2022b) . Lila Mishra et al. (2022a) annotates many of the previously mentioned MWP datasets with Python program rationales.

records.subject: Deep Learning for Mathematical Reasoning
records.missing: Lack of a clear taxonomy of mathematical reasoning tasks and specific capabilities required for deep learning models.
records.quote: there is still a lack of a clear taxonomy of the different types of mathematical reasoning tasks and the specific capabilities required of deep learning models to solve them.

records.subject: Mathematical Reasoning Benchmarks
records.missing: Existing benchmarks lack focus on multi-modal and low-resource settings.
records.quote: We also analyze existing benchmarks and find that there is less focus on multi-modal and low-resource settings

records.subject: Numeracy Representations
records.missing: Current numeracy representations are insufficient, and deep learning methods are inconsistent for mathematical reasoning.
records.quote: Our evidence-based studies suggest that current numeracy representations are insufficient and deep learning methods are inconsistent for mathematical reasoning

records.subject: In-context Learning (ICL)
records.missing: Standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning.
records.quote: such standard few-shot promptings, in which the LLM is given in-context examples of input–output pairs in front of test-time examples, have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning

records.subject: In-context Example Selection
records.missing: It remains an unknown problem which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts.
records.quote: Therefore, which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts is still an unknown problem in the literature.

records.subject: Numeracy Representation
records.missing: Improving numeracy representation using scientific notation and digit-level decomposition remains an open problem.
records.quote: Some recent work suggests that using scientific notation and digit-level decomposition may be helpful in improving numeracy representation, but this remains an open problem.

records.subject: Generalization and Robustness
records.missing: Neural models commonly display generalization and robustness failures on reasoning tasks, such as generalizing to larger numbers or remaining robust to nearby problems.
records.quote: Despite impressive progress, neural models commonly display generalization and robustness failures on reasoning tasks. For example, above we discussed difficulties in generalizing to larger numbers ( Table 5 ) or remaining robust to nearby problems ( Table 6 )

records.subject: Trustworthy Reasoning
records.missing: Language models can still hallucinate statements, produce flawed reasoning, and output wrong answers, necessitating novel approaches for reliable reasoning.
records.quote: Even with recent prompting strategies that provide rationales before making predictions , language models can still hallucinate statements, produce flawed reasoning, and output wrong answers. Consequently, novel approaches that enable more reliable reasoning are needed urgently.

records.subject: Multi-modal Mathematical Reasoning
records.missing: Currently available datasets for multi-modal mathematical reasoning tend to be small, generated from templates, or focus on specific topics.
records.quote: However, currently available datasets in this domain tend to be small , generated from templates , or focus on specific topics .

claims.claim: Ozcan et al. utilized histograms of edge orientations and gradient local binary patterns combined with three-axis accelerometer signals for fall detection, showing higher sensitivity and reduced false alarms compared to accelerometer and camera only methods.

A multi-stream convolutional network was extended for egocentric video activity analysis, and a novel multi-stream LSTM was proposed for wearable sensor data classification, with average and maximum pooling evaluated for score fusion.

Song et al. proposed integrating temporal information into sensor data with similar trajectories and applied the Fisher Kernel framework with Multimodal Fisher Vector (MFV) to fuse sensor and video data for EAR.
Features were extracted using a sliding window on video and inertial data, fused via majority voting, with Random Forest and Support Vector Machine considered for classification.

A hierarchical fusion framework based on deep learning was developed using LSTM and CNN for EAR based on motion sensor data and photo streams at different levels, effectively eliminating negative impacts of sensor differences.

A novel framework using multi-kernel learning (MKL) was proposed to fuse multimodal features, adaptively weighing visual, audio, and sensor features while performing feature/kernel weighting and recognition simultaneously.
Huang et al. proposed a first-view multimodal framework based on knowledge driven, GCN and LSTM, improving EAR performance under few samples and ultra-small datasets.

records.quote: Ozcan et al. [ 103 ] utilized histograms of edge orientations together with the gradient local binary patterns for fall detection, which then combined with three-axis signal of the accelerometer. Experimental results show that the proposed fusion method not only has higher sensitivity, but also significantly reduces the number of false alarms compared with the accelerometer and camera only methods. In [ 121 ] , a multi-stream convolutional network is extended to analysis activity in egocentric videos, meanwhile, a novel multi-stream LSTM is proposed for classifying wearable sensor data. Finally, two score fusion techniques, namely average pooling and maximum pooling, are evaluated to obtain recognition results. Song et al. [ 122 ] proposed a new technique to integrate temporal information into sensor data with similar trajectories. Moreover, the Fisher Kernel framework is applied to fuse sensor and video data for EAR with Multimodal Fisher Vector (MFV). In the work [ 34 ] , features are extracted by applying a sliding window to video and inertial data, Whereafter, using majority voting to fuse the results. For the classification task, methods of Random Forest and Support Vector Machine are taken into consideration. The methods in [ 33 , 32 ] are extensions of [ 34 ] , which use time and frequency domain features for acceleration data, and object information encoding hand interaction for visual data. Experiments are carried out on both feature-level fusion and decision-level fusion, and the latter achieves higher accuracy. In [ 156 ] , a hierarchical fusion framework based on deep learning is developed and implemented, where LSTM and CNN are used for EAR based on motion sensor data and photo streams at different levels, respectively. Experimental results show that the proposed model enables motion sensor data and photo streams to work in the most suitable classification mode, so as to effectively eliminate the negative impact of sensor differences on the fusion results. A novel framework is proposed in [ 4 ] , where multi-kernel learning (MKL) is used to fuse multimodal features in order to adaptively weighs the visual, audio, and sensor features, additionally, feature and kernel weighting and recognition tasks are performed simultaneously. Huang et al. [ 56 ] proposed a first-view multimodal framework based on knowledge driven, GCN and LSTM, which improve the performance of EAR under conditions of few samples and ultra-small datasets.

records.subject: SsDA and MixDA

claims.claim: MixDA creates new training instances by combining multiple training samples, while SsDA only considers a single example.
The feature transformation in SsDA is usually label-invariant, meaning that the newly generated instances have the same target label.
The label combination strategy in MixDA should be carefully designed to align with the feature mixing process.
Most MixDA techniques are domain-agnostic and can be applied to various fields, whereas SsDA techniques are often domain-specific.

records.quote: SsDA and MixDA have three main differences: (i) MixDA creates new training instances by combining multiple training samples, while SsDA only considers a single example; (ii) the feature transformation in SsDA is usually label-invariant, meaning that the newly generated instances have the same target label. In contrast, the label combination strategy in MixDA should be carefully designed to align with the feature mixing process; and (iii) most MixDA techniques are domain-agnostic and can be applied to various fields, whereas SsDA techniques are often domain-specific.

records.subject: MixDA methods

claims.claim: categorizes existing techniques into three main groups: (i) methods that mix training examples from a global perspective, represented by the pioneering work Mixup

records.quote: we propose a novel taxonomy that categorizes existing techniques into three main groups: (i) methods that mix training examples from a global perspective, represented by the pioneering work Mixup ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) ; (ii) approaches that construct new data through the lens of locality , represented by Cutmix ( Yun et al., 2019 ) ; and (iii) other techniques that are based on the principle of mixing but cannot be simply grouped into the above two categories, such as mixing with data reconstruction and integrating multiple MixDA solutions.

records.claim: Mixup and its variants typically develop and apply a global mix scheme to all features, while Cutmix and its adaptations intercept partial features from one instance and paste them on another
records.quote: Mixup and its variants typically develop and apply a global mix scheme to all features. In contrast, Cutmix and its adaptations intercept partial features from one instance and paste them on another, aiming to improve the model’s localization ability.

records.subject: NL2Code benchmarks

claims.claim: Most benchmarks contain a limited number of instances, such as HumanEval and MBPP having 164 and 974 instances respectively, to avoid data leakage.
claims.conditions: hand-written to ensure LLMs have not seen them during training

claims.claim: Most current benchmarks have problem descriptions in English and code solutions in Python.
Several multi-lingual benchmarks have been proposed, covering multiple programming languages or natural languages.

records.quote: We observe that most benchmarks contain a limited number of instances. For example, the widely used HumanEval and MBPP have 164 164 and 974 974 instances, respectively. This is because these benchmarks are typically hand-written to ensure that LLMs have not seen them during training. In the era of large language models, it is crucial to avoid data leakage when creating new benchmarks. Additionally, most current benchmarks have their problem descriptions in English and code solutions in Python. Recently, several multi-lingual benchmarks have been proposed, such as MBXP Athiwaratkun et al. (2022) , HumanEvalX Zheng et al. (2023) , and MultiPL Cassano et al. (2022) , which cover multiple programming languages, and ODEX Wang et al. (2022c) , which covers multiple natural languages.

records.subject: NL2Code metrics

claims.claim: Execution-based evaluation uses metrics like pass@k, n@k, test case average, and execution accuracy, but requires high-quality test cases and only evaluates executable code.
claims.claims_about: pass@k, n@k, test case average, execution accuracy

claims.claim: For non-executable code, metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and CodeBLEU are used, but they cannot precisely evaluate correctness.

records.quote: The above mentioned benchmarks all provide test cases for execution-based evaluation, where metrics such as pass @ k Chen et al. (2021) , n @ k Li et al. (2022b) , test case average Hendrycks et al. (2021) , and execution accuracy Rajkumar et al. (2022) can be used. However, this approach has stringent requirements for the quality of test cases and can only evaluate executable code. For non-executable code, metrics like BLEU Papineni et al. (2002) , ROUGE Lin (2004) , and CodeBLEU Ren et al. (2020) are used, while they can not precisely evaluate the correctness of the code.

claims.claim: In 2018, a video memorability annotation procedure was established, and the first ever large video memorability dataset VideoMem was created.
In 2019, the task ran for a second time using the same dataset allowing participants to learn from the previous year’s task.
In 2020, a new smaller dataset was introduced which included audio for the first time.
In 2021, that dataset was extended, with a second large short-term dataset—Memento10k—being released.

records.quote: In 2018, a video memorability annotation procedure was established, and the first ever large video memorability dataset VideoMem Cohendet et al. (2019) —10,000 short soundless videos with both long-term and short-term memorability scores—was created. Additionally, the first ever analysis of human consistency and video memorability was conducted. In 2019, the task ran for a second time using the same dataset allowing participants to learn from the previous year’s task and carry out comparative analysis of results from one year to the next. In 2020, a new smaller dataset was introduced which included audio for the first time Kiziltepe et al. (2021) . In 2021, that dataset was extended, with a second large short-term dataset—Memento10k Newman et al. (2020) —being released, short-term memorability was sub-categorised into raw and normalised scores, an optional generalisation sub-task was proposed, and a pilot EEG study Sweeney et al. (2021) was conducted.

records.subject: knowledge (internal, external, or hybrid)

claims.claim: Existing work can be grouped into the category of knowledge that they use (i.e., internal, external, or hybrid), where each knowledge category is based on the location from which the knowledge was taken.

records.quote: the existing work can be grouped into the category of knowledge that they use (i.e., internal, external, or hybrid), where each knowledge category is based on the location from which the knowledge was taken

records.subject: Internal knowledge

claims.claim: Internal knowledge is implicit information that is extracted from the dialogue and made explicit.
It can be structured, such as AMR graphs or dependency trees, or unstructured, such as conversation topics or the speaker’s emotional state.

records.quote: Internal knowledge is implicit information that is extracted from the dialogue and made explicit. In simple words, this is information that can be seen as "between the lines" of the dialogue. It can be structured, such as AMR graphs or dependency trees

records.subject: external knowledge

claims.claim: External knowledge is information that is not extracted from the dialogue and exists in an outside source.
It can be structured, such as KGs and knowledge bases (KBs), or unstructured, such as free text, and take the form of triples, table entries, or strings.

records.quote: In contrast, external knowledge is information that is not extracted from the dialogue and exists in an outside source. It can be structured, such as KGs and knowledge bases (KBs), or unstructured, such as free text

records.subject: hybrid knowledge

claims.claim: Hybrid knowledge is a combination of internal and external knowledge.

records.quote: The third, hybrid knowledge , is a combination of internal and external knowledge, such as emotion categories and KGs, topic representations and KBs, or intent vectors, KGs, and free text.

records.subject: privacy-related topics on speech-centric ML

claims.claim: Papers are organized based on privacy threats, mitigation mechanisms, downstream applications, and training paradigms.
Privacy threats are categorized into Property Inference Attacks (PIA), Membership Inference Attacks (MIA), Identity Inference Attacks (IIA), and Content Inference Attacks (CIA).
Privacy mitigation methods are divided into algorithmic solutions and hardware solutions.
Downstream speech applications are categorized into automatic speaker verification, keyword spotting, automatic speech recognition, and speech emotion recognition.
Training paradigms are categorized into centralized learning and federated learning (FL).

records.quote: we organize papers based on privacy threats, mitigation mechanisms, downstream applications, and training paradigms. In the first place, we categorize privacy threats based on privacy attacks, including Property Inference Attacks (PIA), Membership Inference Attacks (MIA), Identity Inference Attacks (IIA), and Content Inference Attacks (CIA). ... we can divide privacy-related literature based on privacy mitigation methods. Specifically, the literature surrounding privacy-preserving speech processing can be categorized into algorithmic solutions and hardware solutions. Moreover, the most studied downstream speech applications related to privacy topics can be categorized into automatic speaker verification, keyword spotting, automatic speech recognition, and speech emotion recognition. Lastly, we discuss the privacy-related speech-centric ML based on the training paradigm: centralized learning and federated learning (FL).

claims.claim: A two-level hierarchical optimization strategy involving local client optimization followed by global optimization and retraining helps adjust to client drift.

claims.claim: Traditional methods are mainly divided into knowledge-based and corpus-based methods.
Knowledge-based methods tend to use common sense knowledge from lexical database sources such as dictionaries, WordNet, and dependency trees.
Corpus-based measures capture the semantic similarity of words and texts calculated from data rather than compiled knowledge rules.
Most corpus-based methods are probabilistic.

records.quote: we formulate three major categories for tampering detection. The first and second class, i.e. Rule-based (Sec. II-C1 ) and Learning-based (Sec. II-C2 ) methods, are categorized based on whether machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) algorithms are utilized to detect tampering clues. On the other hand, we find that some methods gracefully combine the rule-based methods devised by forgery analysts with neural networks, which make them different from methods falling into the previous two categories. As a result, we come up with the third category, i.e. Hybrid Detection Methods (Sec. II-C3 ), alongside the previous two to present readers the whole picture of tampering detection.

records.subject: Methods with Statistical References

claims.claim: Methods with Statistical References refer to forensic methods that require prior knowledge related to the image acquisition chain as detection guidance.

records.subject: face attribute editing

claims.claim: Face attribute editing aims to manipulate specific attributes, e.g., gender and age, of human faces, seen as fine-grained face manipulation.
A series of methods define face attribute editing as a multi-domain image-to-image translation task, taking domain labels as inputs.

claims.conditions: Unlike the above methods which reply on explicit domain labels

records.quote: Instead of synthesizing the complete faces, face attribute editing [ 182 , 151 , 183 , 184 ] aims to manipulate specific attributes, e.g. , gender and age, of human faces, which therefore can be seen as fine-grained face manipulation. Denoting face attributes as different “domains”, a series of methods [ 3 , 185 , 186 ] define face attribute editing as a multi-domain image-to-image translation task. These approaches [ 3 , 187 ] take the domain labels, e.g. , binary vectors, as inputs to translate the images into the target domain. However, [ 188 ] argues that utilizing the target attribution vector is redundant and may even lead to poor results; instead, they directly adopt the difference attribute vectors to provide more valuable guidance. Unlike the above methods which reply on explicit domain labels, other work manipulates the latent representations in 2D [ 189 , 190 , 191 , 192 , 193 , 194 ] or 3D space [ 195 , 196 ] to implicitly control the editing process, leveraging the entangled nature of the GAN latent space.

records.quote: If the attacker can modify what the target agent learns then the attack is defined as a training-time attack. ... Otherwise, if the attacker can act only against an already trained agent, it is defined as a test-time attack.

records.subject: attacker capabilities in RL security

claims.claim: Attackers can perturb the environment, alter specific states, or tamper with sensory inputs to modify the agent’s perception.
claims.conditions: Since the agent’s observations drive both training and inference

claims.claim: Attackers can manipulate actuators such that action performed differs from those chosen by the agent, or modify the reward signal during training to degrade performance.

records.quote: attackers can perturb the environment ( c ⁡ ( ℰ ) c({\mathcal{E}}) ) by adding objects or introducing malicious agents, alter specific states ( c ⁡ ( 𝐬 ) c({\mathbf{s}}) ), or tamper with sensory inputs ( c ⁡ ( 𝐨 ) c({\mathbf{o}}) ) to modify the agent’s perception. They can also manipulate actuators ( c ⁡ ( a ) c({a}) ) such that action performed differs from those chosen by the agent, or modify the reward signal ( c ⁡ ( r ) c({r}) ) during training to degrade performance.

records.subject: attacker knowledge levels

claims.claim: White-box setting enables worst-case evaluations and provides upper bounds on performance degradation.
claims.conditions: If attackers have full knowledge of the system

claims.claim: Adversaries have partial knowledge, such as observing states and rewards but lacking details of the RL algorithm.
The attacker has no internal knowledge and relies solely on external observations of inputs and outputs.

records.quote: If attackers have full knowledge of the system, the attack is termed a white-box . Though unrealistic in practice, this setting enables worst-case evaluations and provides upper bounds on performance degradation. In a gray-box setting, adversaries have partial knowledge—for instance, they may observe states and rewards but lack details of the RL algorithm. Finally, in a black-box setting, the attacker has no internal knowledge and relies solely on external observations of inputs and outputs

claims.claim: Attackers often exploit transferability by crafting attacks on a surrogate RL system and deploying them against the target.

records.quote: In gray- and black-box settings, attackers often exploit transferability [ 44 ] , crafting attacks on a surrogate RL system and deploying them against the target.

records.section: V-A Categorizing the Attacks against RL

records.claim: The Enchanting Attack uses a generative model and planning algorithm to guide the agent towards a specific target state.
records.quote: One of the attacks proposed in [ 63 ] : Enchanting Attack, where the attacker focuses on luring the DRL agent to a specific, pre-determined target state using the generative model and planning algorithm that generates a sequence of actions to guide the agent towards the target.

records.claim: The Antagonist Attack is domain-agnostic and applicable to multi-agent environments, but its evaluation was conducted in a single-agent environment.
records.quote: One of the two attacks in [ 37 ] is Antagonist Attack, which is domain-agnostic and general enough to be applied to a multi-agent environment; however, the evaluation is done single-agent environment.

records.subject: attacks on autonomous driving (AD)

claims.claim: Most attacks target end-to-end systems at test time, aiming to force lane departures or unsafe maneuvers
Training-time threats include policy poisoning, which manipulates rewards to misguide planning
Training-time threats include backdoor attacks that target either traffic optimization algorithms or vehicle behaviors

records.quote: Most attacks target end-to-end systems at test time, aiming to force lane departures or unsafe maneuvers [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] , sometimes via physical perturbations such as painted road lines or printed artifacts. Others exploit sensor inputs, environment responses, or online image streams [ 71 ] , with some leveraging sparse perturbations to evade detection [ 72 ] . Training-time threats include policy poisoning, which manipulates rewards to misguide planning [ 21 ] , and backdoor attacks that target either traffic optimization algorithms [ 19 ] or vehicle behaviors [ 61 ] .

records.quote: Most are not tested on actual cars, likely due to the high cost of AVs, and only a few consider actions feasible in the physical world [ 36 , 38 ] .
