records.subject: Adversarial RL Timeline

claims.claim: The first attacks against RL were test-time integrity awards proposed in 2017, inspired by attacks proposed between 2004 and 2005 against ML classifiers.
The first training-time poisoning attack against RL was proposed in 2017, inspired by an attack proposed in 2012 against the Support Vector Machine.
The first paper on targeted poisoning attack in 2018 and backdoor poisoning attack in 2020 were proposed, both inspired by articles proposed in 2017.
claims.claims_about: targeted poisoning attack, backdoor poisoning attack

claims.claim: The only attack that violates the privacy of RL systems performs stealing of the model, was proposed recently in 2021, inspired by an attack previously proposed against ML classifiers in 2016.
Attacks that aim to slow down the system have been proposed against ML systems but have never been demonstrated against RL systems.

records.quote: The first attacks against RL were test-time integrity awards [ 63 , 43 ] , proposed in 2017 and were able to make the system misbehave when a carefully crafted sample was provided as input to the system. These attacks are inspired by those [ 83 , 84 ] that were proposed more than ten years before, between 2004 and 2005, against ML classifiers that misclassified carefully crafted adversarial samples. For example, misclassifying a spam email as legitimate. The first training-time poisoning attack against RL was also proposed in 2017 [ 62 ] . The goal of this attack was to make the system unable to work correctly, specifically by manipulating the target policy, causing a denial of service. In this case, the attack is also inspired by an attack [ 85 ] proposed a long time before (2012) against ML classifiers and in particular against the Support Vector Machine, affecting its ability to learn to correctly classify the samples. In 2018 and 2020, researchers proposed the first integrity-violation train-time attacks against RL. In particular, the first paper on targeted poisoning attack  [ 53 ] in 2018 and backdoor poisoning attack  [ 50 ] in 2020 were proposed. Both were inspired by articles proposed in 2017 [ 86 , 87 ] where former aimed to misclassify test samples by manipulating a few training samples while latter made the classifier learn to misclassify all samples containing a specific trigger. The only attack that violates the privacy of RL systems [ 88 ] performs stealing of the model, was proposed recently in 2021, is inspired by an attack previously proposed against ML classifiers [ 89 ] in 2016. Whereas against ML, also an attack to understand if some data were employed to train the model [ 88 ] and an attack to obtain a copy of the model [ 89 ] were proposed, respectively in 2015 and 2016. The attacks that aim to slow down the system have been proposed against ML systems [ 90 , 91 ] but have never been demonstrated against RL systems.

records.subject: RL defense methods

claims.claim: All existing RL defense methods have adapted techniques that were previously devised for ML classification tasks.

They can be divided into three main categories: a) those that try to counteract an existing attacks, i.e. reactive defenses, and b) those that act to prevent future attacks, i.e. proactive defenses, and c) those that detect the attack and provide proactive solutions, hybrid.

records.quote: All existing RL defense methods have adapted techniques that were previously devised for ML classification tasks. They can be divided into three main categories: a) those that try to counteract an existing attacks, i.e. reactive defenses, and b) those that act to prevent future attacks, i.e. proactive defenses [ 17 ] , and c) those that detect the attack and provide proactive solutions, hybrid .

records.subject: Detection ( det. )

claims.claim: The goal is to identify whether the input to the RL agent (e.g., observations, environment dynamics, etc.) has been adversarially perturbed or is out-of-distribution.

records.quote: Detection ( det. ): The goal is to identify whether the input to the RL agent (e.g., observations, environment dynamics, etc.) has been adversarially perturbed or is out-of-distribution.

records.subject: Sanitization ( san. )

claims.claim: It is a proactive train time defense that preprocesses the input to remove adversarial perturbations before feeding them into the RL system.

records.quote: Sanitization ( san. ): It is a proactive train time defense that preprocesses the input to remove adversarial perturbations before feeding them into the RL system.

records.subject: Adversarial training ( adv. tr. )

claims.claim: Iteratively re-train the system on the simulated attacks.
These defenses are heuristic and do not have formal guarantees on convergence.

records.quote: Adversarial training ( adv. tr. ): Iteratively re-train the system on the simulated attacks. These defenses are heuristic and do not have formal guarantees on convergence.

records.subject: Game Theory ( game th. )

claims.claim: Model the interaction between the agent and adversary as a game (Nash equilibrium [ 94 ] or Stackelberg game [ 95 ] ) and solve the robust policy, e.g. using minimax optimization.
They are more principled than adversarial training; however, they are computationally costly.

records.quote: Game Theory ( game th. ): Model the interaction between the agent and adversary as a game (Nash equilibrium [ 94 ] or Stackelberg game [ 95 ] ) and solve the robust policy, e.g. using minimax optimization. They are more principled than adversarial training; however, they are computationally costly.

records.subject: Regularization ( reg. )

claims.claim: Adds constraints or penalty terms during training to penalize agent’s sensitivity to input’s perturbations or choosing the best action considering a possible worst-case perturbation of the input.

records.quote: Regularization ( reg. ): Adds constraints or penalty terms during training to penalize agent’s sensitivity to input’s perturbations or choosing the best action considering a possible worst-case perturbation of the input.

records.subject: Distillation ( dist. )

claims.claim: This technique was originally proposed for model compression [ 96 ].
Transfer knowledge from a robust, larger network, the teacher model, to a smaller or less complex, the student model, often smoothing decision boundaries.

records.quote: Distillation ( dist. ): This technique was originally proposed for model compression [ 96 ]. Transfer knowledge from a robust, larger network, the teacher model, to a smaller or less complex, the student model, often smoothing decision boundaries.

records.subject: Ensemble ( ens. )

claims.claim: Use multiple agents, i.e. policy or value functions, and aggregate their outputs to make decisions more robust against perturbations or adversarial attacks.

records.subject: Student's FER databases

claims.claim: The database in [40] contains spontaneous expressions with 4 classes (Not engaged, Nominally engaged, Engaged in task, Very engaged), participants are Asian-American, Caucasian-American, African-American (25 female), acquired via IPad camera at 30cm, labeled by students from various disciplines, with 34 participants.

The database in [10] contains spontaneous expressions with 5 classes (Joviality, Surprise, Concentration, Confusion, Fatigue), participants are Asian, acquired via 1080p HD camera at front of classroom during a 6-minute video, self-labeled, with 200 images and 23 participants.

The database in [45] contains spontaneous expressions with 4 classes (Frustration, Boredom, Engagement, Excitement), ethnicity N/A, acquired via computer webcam every 5 seconds, labeled using Emotiv Epoc EEG technology, with 730 images.

The database in [46] contains spontaneous expressions with 5 classes (Confusion, Distraction, Enjoyment, Neutral, Fatigue), participants are Chinese (29 male, 53 female), acquired via computer cameras, labeled by participants and external coders, with 1,274 videos, 30,184 images, and 82 participants.

The database in [38] contains posed and spontaneous expressions with 14 classes (7 Ekman basic emotions, 3 learning-centered emotions: Frustration, confusion, boredom, and Neutral), participants are Indian, acquired via frontal posed expressions, labeled using semi-automatic annotation and manual review, with 4000 samples.

claims.claim: Influence estimators only approximate the true influence and are commonly used in practice.

records.quote: Since measuring influence exactly may be intractable or unnecessary, influence estimators – which only approximate the true influence – are commonly used in practice. As with any approximation, influence estimation requires making trade-offs, and the various influence estimators balance these design choices differently. This in turn leads influence estimators to make different assumptions and rely on different mathematical formulations.

records.subject: retraining-based influence analysis

claims.claim: The basic intuition of retraining-based influence analysis is to train a model with and without some instance and define influence as the difference in behavior.
The retraining-based framework makes no assumptions about the learning environment, which is a primary advantage.
Retraining-based influence analysis has high (sometimes prohibitive) computational cost.

records.quote: one method to measure influence just trains a model with and without some instance; influence is then defined as the difference in these two models’ behavior. This basic intuition is the foundation of retraining-based influence analysis... Observe that the retraining-based framework makes no assumptions about the learning environment. In fact, this simplicity is one of the primary advantages of retraining-based influence. ... However, retraining’s flexibility comes at the expense of high (sometimes prohibitive) computational cost.

Dynamic, gradient-based influence estimators reconstruct the training data’s influence by studying model parameters throughout training, e.g., θ ( 0 ) ; … ; θ ( T ) {\theta^{(0)}\mathchar 59\relax\ldots\mathchar 59\relax\theta^{(T)}} .

records.quote: Static, gradient-based methods – discussed first – estimate the effect of retraining by studying gradients w.r.t. final model parameters θ ( T ) \theta^{(T)} . records.subject: medical summarization task

claims.claim: Report Summarization refers to the summarization of notes or reports generated by a medical professional during the encounter with patients.
Health Record Summarization is defined as the multi-document summarization task where given a sequence of input documents, we have to generate a summary.
CHQ Summarization can be defined as the task of summarization of these medical questions by replacing input data D in Equation 1 with CHQ.
Medical Dialogue Summarization can be defined as the process of summarizing a conversation over a digital platform or a physical encounter between a medical professional and a patient.
The aim of biomedical summarization systems is to summarize and present important and relevant medical facts and information from long articles to medical professionals.

records.subject: XAI

claims.claim: XAI methods compute an explanation of the ML model’s behaviour by mapping the input of a black box model to its output.
claims.conditions: As the explanation method is external to the ML model, faithfulness is not guaranteed.

claims.claim: A common theme in XAI is the attribution of a metric that represents the impact of a specific input characterization, frequently referred to as the attribution value of an input feature.
Other innovative themes exist in XAI, like counterfactual explanation methods or explanations methods based on Inductive Logic Programming (ILP).
claims.claims_about: counterfactual explanation methods, Inductive Logic Programming (ILP)

records.quote: While IML tries to uncover the whole decision-making process of the ML model, XAI is about mapping the input of a black box model to its output. That way, XAI methods compute an explanation of the ML model’s behaviour. As the explanation method is external to the ML model, faithfulness is not guaranteed. However, the quality of a XAI method is measured by how faithful their explanations reflect the model’s behaviour. The inside reasoning and processing of the black box model are not be made transparent by the XAI method. A common theme in XAI is the attribution of a metric that represents the impact of a specific input characterization, frequently referred to as the attribution value of an input feature. The attribution tells how important an input feature is for or against a classification. Such methods are so-called attribution methods [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 ] . Other innovative themes exist in XAI, like counterfactual explanation methods [ 51 ] or explanations methods based on Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) [ 52 ] .

records.subject: CAI

claims.claim: CAI serves four reasons: justifying output, identifying risks/flaws, enabling debugging/improvement, and uncovering unknown rules.

records.quote: CAI serves the following four reasons. (1) The CAI model is supposed to justify its output [ 43 , 44 ] . One possible application of this is to verify that the resulting output aligns with the ethical principles of a particular moral framework [ 43 , 44 ] . (2) Furthermore, explanations help to identify risks and flaws of an AI model. A possible risk is the Clever Hans bias described by Lapuschkin et al. [45] . They describe an image classifier that classifies horses correctly because all pictures with horses have a particular watermark on them. The explanation of the classifier uncovers this flaw [ 43 , 44 ] . (3) Finding risks and flaws of an AI model enable researchers or developers to debug and improve the model [ 43 , 44 ] . (4) In addition, producing explanations for an AI model might uncover unknown rules discovered by the AI model [ 43 , 44 ] .

records.claim: need to extract knowledge from both the networks simultaneously for accurate inference
records.conditions: in contrast with most regular GNNs that consider only a single network
records.quote: Thus, GNN methods for SocialRS need to extract knowledge from both the networks simultaneously for accurate inference. This is in contrast with most regular GNNs that consider only a single network.

records.claim: fuse features along with network information
records.conditions: valuable input features in the two networks, such as user/item attributes, item knowledge/relation, and group information
records.quote: Thus, methods fuse features along with network information in GNN-based SocialRS.

records.claim: rely heavily on their GNN encoders, which aim to represent users and items into low-dimensional embeddings
records.quote: The performance of GNN-based SocialRS methods relies heavily on their GNN encoders, which aim to represent users and items into low-dimensional embeddings.

records.claim: employ the graph attention neural network (GANN) to differentiate each user’s preference for items or each user’s influence on their social friends
records.quote: For instance, many SocialRS methods employ the graph attention neural network (GANN) ( Veličković et al., 2018 ) to differentiate each user’s preference for items or each user’s influence on their social friends.

records.claim: use the graph recurrent neural networks (GRNN) to model the sequential behaviors of users
records.quote: On the other hand, some methods ( Sun et al., 2020 ; Yan et al., 2022 ; Gu et al., 2021 ; Narang et al., 2021 ; Niu et al., 2021 ) use the graph recurrent neural networks (GRNN) ( Peng et al., 2017 ; Zayats and Ostendorf, 2018 ) to model the sequential behaviors of users.

records.claim: need to simultaneously consider the characteristics of user-item interactions and user-user social relations
records.conditions: in contrast with GNN encoders for non-SocialRS that model only user-item interactions
records.quote: It should be noted that GNN encoders for SocialRS need to simultaneously consider the characteristics of user-item interactions and user-user social relations. This is in contrast with GNN encoders for non-SocialRS that model only user-item interactions.

records.claim: employ well-known loss functions, such as mean squared error (MSE), Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR), and cross-entropy (CE), to reconstruct user behaviors
records.conditions: to reflect users’ tastes and items’ characteristics in the embeddings
records.quote: To this end, SocialRS methods employ well-known loss functions, such as mean squared error (MSE), Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR) ( Rendle et al., 2009 ) , and cross-entropy (CE), to reconstruct user behaviors.

records.claim: have additionally employed auxiliary loss functions such as self-supervised loss and group-based loss
records.conditions: to mitigate the data sparsity problem

records.subject: loss functions

claims.claim: MSE has Low complexity, learns continuous ratings, and is sensitive to outliers.
BPR has Low complexity, learns rankings between items, and cannot handle continuous ratings.
CE has Low complexity, is suited for classification, and cannot handle continuous ratings.
Hinge has Low complexity, offers faster convergence, and cannot handle continuous ratings.
Social LP has Low complexity, provides more suitable social embeddings, and involves multi-objective trade-off.
SSL has High complexity, provides more informed representations, and requires expensive pre-processing.
Group has Low complexity, provides group-level representations, and groups form for specific items (common interests).
Adv has High complexity, provides more robust representations, and suffers from adversarial instability and cost.
Path has High complexity, predicts social influence propagation, and involves a complicated auxiliary task.
KD has High complexity, reduces overfitting, and requires training multiple models.
Sentiment has High complexity, uses user sentiment-weighed ratings, and involves a complex sentiment classification task.
Policy Net. has High complexity, assigns importance weights to each component, and involves expensive weight allocation.

claims.claim: encoders of GNN-based SocialRS are grouped into 8 categories: graph convolutional network (GCN), lightweight GCN (LightGCN), graph attention neural networks (GANN), heterogeneous GNN (HetGNN), graph recurrent neural networks (GRNN), hypergraph neural networks (HyperGNN), graph autoencoder (GAE), and hyperbolic GNN.

records.quote: We group the encoders of GNN-based SocialRS into 8 categories: graph convolutional network (GCN), lightweight GCN (LightGCN), graph attention neural networks (GANN), heterogeneous GNN (HetGNN), graph recurrent neural networks (GRNN), hypergraph neural networks (HyperGNN), graph autoencoder (GAE), and hyperbolic GNN.

records.claim: DiffNet uses GCN to obtain user social and interaction embeddings based on U-U and U-I graphs.
records.quote: For instance, DiffNet ( Wu et al., 2019a ) obtains a user p i p_{i} ’s social embedding 𝐮 i S \mathbf{u}_{i}^{S} (resp. interaction embedding 𝐮 i I \mathbf{u}_{i}^{I} ) by performing GCN with k k -layers (resp. 1 1 -layer) based on the U-U graph (resp. U-I graph).

records.subject: loss functions of GNN-based SocialRS

claims.claim: Primary loss functions are grouped into 4 categories: Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR), mean squared error (MSE), cross-entropy (CE), and hinge loss.

Auxiliary loss functions are grouped into 8 categories: social link prediction (LP) loss, self-supervised loss (SSL), group-based loss, adversarial (Adv) loss, path-based loss, knowledge distillation (KD) loss, sentiment-aware loss, and policy-network-based (Policy Net) loss.

records.quote: we first group the primary loss functions of GNN-based SocialRS into 4 categories: Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR) ( Rendle et al., 2009 ) , mean squared error (MSE), cross-entropy (CE), and hinge loss. In addition, we found that some works additionally employ auxiliary loss functions. Thus, we further group these loss functions into 8 categories: social link prediction (LP) loss, self-supervised loss (SSL), group-based loss, adversarial (Adv) loss, path-based loss, knowledge distillation (KD) loss, sentiment-aware loss, and policy-network-based (Policy Net) loss.

records.subject: semantic SLAM and Cartographer SLAM

claims.claim: Semantic SLAM incorporates higher-level scene interpretation and enhances users’ contextual awareness.
Cartographer SLAM provides SLAM in 2D and 3D across various platforms and sensor configurations.

records.quote: The utilization of semantic SLAM and Cartographer SLAM signifies a recent trend towards leveraging advanced spatial understanding and mapping capabilities for visually impaired navigation. Semantic SLAM incorporates higher-level scene interpretation and enhances users’ contextual awareness. On the other hand, Cartographer SLAM provides SLAM in 2D and 3D across various platforms and sensor configurations, offering innovative solutions to tackle the diverse challenges associated with BVI navigation.

records.subject: User-based evaluations

claims.claim: Involved 9 BVI participants on a university campus; feedback varied on pleasantness, annoyance, precision, quickness, and overall appreciation of sonification.
Involved 2 BVI and 3 blindfolded participants in a lab; no overall satisfaction score, but details on task success rates, completion times, and verbal/haptic feedback provided.
Involved 5 BVI and 3 blindfolded participants; achieved user satisfaction scores between six and nine out of ten.
Evaluated with 10 blindfolded participants; noted improvements in acceptance and trust levels.
Involved 8 blindfolded participants in a room; found moderate to high satisfaction, with users finding the system acceptable and useful for indoor navigation.
Involved 12 BVI and 12 blindfolded participants; novice and expert users noted usability challenges due to weight, but confidence and workload improved.
Involved 8 BVI participants; participants found the proposed route easy to navigate, with low perceived difficulty and medium confidence, and most intend to use it again.
Involved 20 BVI participants; positive feedback on usability and navigation, desire for detailed tutorials, satisfaction with daily use, but challenges with multi-floor navigation.
Involved 4 BVI participants; all subjects found haptic instructions intuitive, enhancing safety and reducing hesitation compared to audio, though some suggested design improvements.
Involved 7 blindfolded participants; users found the wayfinding function useful, but discomfort due to weight is a significant concern.
Involved 3 BVI participants at two crosswalks; verbal instructions were intuitive and easy-to-understand, enhancing street crossing safety.
Involved 7 BVI participants in an unfamiliar building; high satisfaction with PathFinder’s navigation assistance, intersection detection, and audio feedback.
Involved 6 blindfolded participants in a configurable room; high confidence, ease of use, and performance rated positively; verbal overview and haptics well-received.

claims.claims_about: Traditional methods for planning domain representation

claims.claim: AI planning techniques often employ domain-independent action description languages like the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL).
Temporal logic approaches utilize formalisms such as linear temporal logic (LTL), signal temporal logic (STL), and metric temporal logic (MTL).

records.quote: Traditional methods for planning domain representation have been adopted from both the AI planning and temporal logic communities [ 23 ] . These methods generally involve the use of logic. Sec. III-A presents AI planning techniques that often employ domain-independent action description languages like the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), which are widely interfaced with state-of-the-art task planners. Temporal logic approaches (Sec. III-B ), utilizing formalisms such as linear temporal logic (LTL) [ 40 , 41 ] , signal temporal logic (STL) [ 42 ] , and metric temporal logic (MTL) [ 43 ] , have been extensively used to express time-dependent behaviors and constraints.

records.subject: MLLMs

claims.claim: MLLMs with encoder-only architecture can effectively handle long-range dependencies within the input sequences, making them well-suited for the analysis and classification of textual content, including tasks like sentiment analysis and named entity recognition.
MLLMs with decoder-only architecture are mainly designed to generate sequences of language texts. They predict the next token based on contextual information from the current and preceding steps.
MLLMs with encoder-decoder architecture enable themselves to process sequential data and generate accurate and coherent outputs that excel in tasks such as text generation, and summarization.

records.quote: MLLMs can be categorized into three groups based on the underlying transformer structure: • Encoder-only (e.g., BERT ): MLLMs with encoder-only architecture can effectively handle long-range dependencies within the input sequences, making them well-suited for the analysis and classification of textual content, including tasks like sentiment analysis and named entity recognition. • Decoder-only (e.g., GPT): MLLMs with decoder-only architecture are mainly designed to generate sequences of language texts. They predict the next token based on contextual information from the current and preceding steps. • Encoder-decoder hybrid (e.g., GLM): MLLMs with encoder-decoder architecture enable themselves to process sequential data and generate accurate and coherent outputs that excel in tasks such as text generation, and summarization.

records.subject: multilingual representation alignment

claims.claim: The taxonomy of multilingual representation alignment consists of static, contextual, and combined approaches.
Static multilingual representations are attained through learning a mapping matrix to align two monolingual embedding spaces.
Contextual representations can be achieved by both mapping and joint approaches, with the latter being supported by MLLMs.
Combined methods were proposed to take advantage of both static and contextual information to achieve even better alignment.

records.quote: Figure 5: Taxonomy of multilingual representation alignment that consists of static, contextual, and combined approaches. In addition, we also summarize the factors that affect alignments. ... Static multilingual representations are attained through learning a mapping matrix to align two monolingual embedding spaces, while contextual ones can be achieved by both mapping and joint approaches, with the latter being supported by MLLMs. To achieve even better alignment, combined methods were proposed to take advantage of both static and contextual information.

claims.claim: Combined multilingual approaches are divided into two paradigms: From Static to Contextual (S2C) and From Contextual to Static (C2S).

records.quote: The existing combined multilingual approaches can be divided into two paradigms: (1) From Static to Contextual (S2C), leveraging static information to induce better contextual multilingual alignment [ 113 ] ; (2) From Contextual to Static (C2S), leveraging contextual information to induce better static multilingual alignment [ 114 , 115 ] .

records.subject: debiasing techniques for MLLMs

claims.claim: Current debiasing techniques for MLLMs can be broadly categorized into model debiasing and data debiasing.
Model debiasing techniques rely on refining MLLMs’ inner settings like pre-training parameters, fine-tuning datasets, and representations.
Data debiasing focuses on addressing bias within the input training data of MLLMs.

records.quote: Current debiasing techniques for MLLMs can be broadly categorized into model debiasing and data debiasing . Model debiasing techniques rely on refining MLLMs’ inner settings like pre-training parameters, fine-tuning datasets, and representations, while data debiasing focuses on addressing bias within the input training data of MLLMs.

records.subject: existing methods for debiasing models

claims.claim: Methods are categorized into four lines: representation based, pre-training based, fine-tuning based, and prompt based methods.

records.quote: The existing methods for debiasing models can be categorized into four lines according to their debiasing stage: representation based methods, pre-training based methods, fine-tuning based methods, and prompt based methods.

records.subject: Data Debiasing

records.subject: traffic flow prediction

claims.claim: Traditional time series methods like ARIMA, SVR, and GBDT are limited in dealing with dynamic transportation networks and live flows.
Early continual learning works addressed concept drift in non-stationary data.
Recent works combined graph neural networks (GNNs) and CL to perform traffic flow prediction, focusing on catastrophic forgetting.

records.quote: There is a long history and many well-studied models on urban traffic flow prediction, from traditional time series methods, such as Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) [ 85 ] , Support Vector Regression (SVR) [ 86 ] and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) [ 87 ] , to deep learning methods [ 88 , 89 , 90 ] . Such models are mainly devoted to solving static data and thus become very limited in dealing with dynamic transportation networks and live flows. ... In early works, CL was used to solve the concept drift problem in non-stationary data [ 18 , 69 ] . ... More recent works have combined graph neural networks (GNNs) and CL to perform traffic flow prediction. These works centered more on solving the catastrophic forgetting problem.

records.subject: recommender system applications

claims.claim: Many studies utilized hypergraphs consisting of item nodes and user hyperedges, where all items a user interacted with were connected by a hyperedge.
When sessions were available, hyperedges connected item nodes by their context window.
claims.claims_about: Wang et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022a

claims.claim: Zhang et al. (2021) incorporated user- and group-level hypergraphs.
Ji et al. (2020) constructed a hypergraph with item nodes and a hypergraph with user nodes, where their hyperedges were inferred from heuristic-based algorithms.
Other studies incorporated learnable hypergraph structure.
claims.claims_about: Xia et al., 2022b; Xia et al., 2022a

records.quote: For recommender system applications, many studies utilized hypergraphs consisting of item nodes (being recommended) and user hyperedges (receiving recommendations). For instance, all items that a user interacted with were connected by a hyperedge ( Wang et al., 2020 ). When sessions were available, hyperedges connected item nodes by their context window ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Xia et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022a ). Some studies leveraged multiple hypergraphs. For instance, Zhang et al. (2021) incorporated user- and group-level hypergraphs. Ji et al. (2020) constructed a hypergraph with item nodes and a hypergraph with user nodes, where their hyperedges were inferred from heuristic-based algorithms. In contrast, other studies incorporated learnable hypergraph structure ( Xia et al., 2022b ; Xia et al., 2022a ).

claims.claim: HNNs have been applied to predict interactions or associations among molecular-level structures, formulated as a hyperedge prediction task.

records.subject: Game Taxonomy for LLMGA Design

claims.claim: Action games pose the core challenge of low-latency response, requiring fast action and hybrid architectures.
Adventure games pose the core challenge of stateful world modeling, pushing agents to develop memory structures.
Role-playing games pose the key challenge of role fidelity, shaping agent design toward embedding role profiles.
Strategy games pose the central challenge of opponent-aware planning, requiring multi-step reasoning and opponent modeling.
Simulation games pose the challenge of dynamics fidelity, ensuring behaviors remain credible and human-like.
Sandbox games pose the challenge of open-ended goal progression, driving designs for self-directed goals and skill accumulation.

records.quote: we identify six representative game genres, each posing distinct design challenges for LLM-based agents. (1) Action games... The core challenge is low-latency response... (2) Adventure games... The challenge is stateful world modeling... (3) Role-playing games... The key challenge is role fidelity... (4) Strategy games... Their central challenge is opponent-aware planning... (5) Simulation games... The challenge is dynamics fidelity... (6) Sandbox games... The challenge is open-ended goal progression...

records.subject: Gameplay taxonomy

claims.claim: Action games are associated with low-latency response and environments like Atari 2600 games, Procgen, ViZDoom, DeepMind Lab, and Street Fighter.
Adventure games are associated with stateful world modeling and environments like TextWorld, Jericho, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Red Dead Redemption II, and STARLING.
Role-playing games are associated with role fidelity and environments like AvalonBench, Werewolf, Diplomacy, Among Us, SOTOPIA, and clembench.
Strategy games are associated with opponent-aware planning and environments like Chess/Go, Poker, Pokémon Battles, StarCraft II, Card Games, and LLM-PySC2.
Simulation games are associated with dynamics fidelity and environments like Generative Agents, Humanoid Agents, AgentSims, LyfeGame, CivRealm, Artificial Leviathan, IndoorWorld, and Moltbook.
Sandbox games are associated with open-ended goal progression and environments like Minecraft, MineDojo, Crafter, Plancraft, and UnrealZoo.

records.subject: instruction-guided reasoning

claims.claim: Chain-of-thought guides the model to articulate intermediate steps before arriving at an answer.
Search-based reasoning explores multiple reasoning paths in parallel and selects among them to ensure consistency.
Reflective reasoning iteratively improves reasoning across steps by incorporating internal self-critique or external signals.

records.quote: The first mechanism is chain-of-thought , which guides the model to articulate intermediate steps before arriving at an answer. The second is search-based reasoning , which explores multiple reasoning paths in parallel and selects among them to ensure consistency. The third is reflective reasoning , which iteratively improves reasoning across steps by incorporating internal self-critique or external signals.

records.subject: fine-tuning paradigms

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning involves agents imitating expert demonstrations to acquire reasoning behaviors.
Reinforcement learning updates policies or value models to optimize reasoning with task rewards.
Preference optimization contrasts preferred and dispreferred generations to bias reasoning toward desirable outcomes.

records.quote: The first mechanism is supervised fine-tuning , where agents imitate expert demonstrations to acquire reasoning behaviors. The second is reinforcement learning , which updates policies or value models to optimize reasoning with task rewards. The third is preference optimization , which contrasts preferred and dispreferred generations to bias reasoning toward desirable outcomes.

records.subject: perception and action interfaces

claims.claim: Perception interfaces handle textual, symbolic, and visual observations; action interfaces ground LLM outputs into high-level, low-level, and code-based actions.

records.quote: On the input side, the perception interface determines how raw game states are abstracted into representations that can be processed by the LLM, handling textual , symbolic , and visual observations. On the output side, the action interface ensures that the model’s decisions are translated into admissible in-game operations by grounding the LLM outputs into high-level , low-level , and code-based actions.
records.section: 6. Perception and Action Interfaces of LLMGA

records.subject: Gameplay Taxonomy for LLMGA Design

claims.claim: Action games require low-latency response, challenging agents to reconcile slow LLM deliberation with real-time play demands.
Adventure games highlight stateful world modeling, depending on maintaining coherent memories of evolving environments and quests.
Role-playing games raise the issue of role fidelity, requiring agents to sustain consistent personas and align dialogue with character identity.
Strategy games emphasize opponent-aware planning, focusing on anticipating adversaries' intentions under imperfect information.
Simulation games emphasize dynamics fidelity, evaluating if agents exhibit behaviors faithful to governing simulation dynamics.
Sandbox games expose the challenge of open-ended goal progression, requiring agents to generate objectives and accumulate reusable skills.

records.quote: Action games require low-latency response... Adventure games highlight stateful world modeling... Role-playing games raise the issue of role fidelity... records.subject: Types of digital forgetting

claims.claim: General forgetting requests involve removing documents containing personal information from search results, as implemented by services like Google Search.
claims.conditions: The implementation revolves around removing documents present on the internet and not published by the data subjects themselves.

claims.claim: Item removal requests target the forgetting of one or more specific data points or samples contained within the model.
claims.conditions: Straightforward for models dealing with tabular or image data where data points are precisely defined.

claims.claim: Feature or concept removal requests aim to make the model forget all information about a given subject, which may be spread across different sentences and documents.
claims.conditions: An example is making a model forget everything about the Harry Potter books.

claims.claim: Class removal requests consist of removing all information about a whole class from a model, such as making a facial recognition model unable to identify a specific person.
claims.conditions: A trivial approach is zeroing out logits corresponding to appropriate classes during inference, feasible only in a black-box setting.

claims.claim: Task removal requests attempt to make fine-tuned LLMs forget one or more specific tasks they have been taught to perform, such as summarization or sentiment analysis.
claims.conditions: LLMs are pre-trained on generic tasks and then fine-tuned for specific tasks.

records.conditions: limited access to the GPT-2 training data (through colleagues)
records.quote: They conducted attacks on GPT-2, which is a closed model (both in parameters and training data), but had limited access to the GPT-2 training data (through colleagues) to verify their findings.

records.claim: The baseline attack generates 200,000 samples of unconditioned text using top-k sampling and ranks them based on perplexity assigned by the LLM.
records.quote: Their proposed baseline attack is to generate 200,000 samples of unconditioned text with a generative model, beginning each sample with a special beginning-of-sequence token. Sequences are generated using a top- k k sampling strategy until an ending-of-sequence token is reached. The samples are then ranked based on the perplexity assigned to each sequence by the LLM.

records.claim: One refinement involves changing the temperature during sequence generation, starting high and reducing it progressively to 1 to explore paths and follow seen data.
records.quote: The first one consists in changing the temperature during sequence generation, starting with a high temperature and reducing it progressively until it reaches a value of 1 1 . This allows the LLM to first explore different paths in the generation of the first tokens, and then follow a clearer sequence of (possibly) seen data.

records.claim: Another refinement conditions text generation with data from the internet, exploiting potential intersections between the training dataset and attacker knowledge.
records.quote: Their second approach consists in conditioning the text generation with data from the internet. Note that LLMs are pre-trained on big datasets from publicly accessible data on the internet and thus using data from the same sources could mean that there are intersections between the training dataset and the attacker knowledge.

records.claim: Metrics used include perplexity, ratio of log-perplexity between generating and different models, ratio of log-perplexity over zlib compression, entropy, ratio of perplexities between generated and lowercased samples, and minimum perplexity across 50-token sliding windows.
records.quote: Regarding metrics, the authors use the following ones: perplexity as in the baseline attack, the ratio of the log-perplexity assigned to the sample by the generating model over the log-perplexity assigned to the sample by a different model (mimicking the shadow-model approach by Shokri et al., (2017) ), the ratio of the log-perplexity over the zlib compression library, the entropy of the sample, the ratio of perplexities between the generated sample and a lowercased version of the same sample, and the minimum perplexity across any 50-token long sliding windows.

records.claim: Exact sequences from training data are returned, including personal data, copyrighted material, and security-related information; bigger models tend to leak more exact sequences.
records.quote: The authors show that exact sequences from the training data are returned from the model, including personal data such as names and contact information, copyrighted material such as news pieces, and potentially security-related information, such as logs and configuration files. The work suggests that bigger models tend to leak more exact sequences.

records.claim: Nasr et al. (2023) executed attacks on open-source and semi-open LLMs where adversaries have access to the training dataset or enough information to build a similar one.
records.conditions: adversaries have access to the training dataset or at least enough information to build a similar dataset
records.quote: Nasr et al., (2023) follow up on the work by Carlini et al., (2021) by executing attacks on open-source and semi-open large language models. The key difference in this work is that the adversaries have access to the training dataset or at least enough information to build a similar dataset.

records.claim: Nasr et al. (2023) confirmed that larger and more capable models are more vulnerable to data extraction attacks.
records.quote: The authors confirm the findings of Carlini et al., (2021) , including the observation that larger and more capable models are more vulnerable to data extraction attacks.

records.claim: Attacks on ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) using the same approach as Carlini et al. did not make the models leak any information.
records.quote: Then, they conduct attacks on ChatGPT (with gpt-3.5-turbo) and find that the same approach does not make the models leak any information.

records.claim: A divergence attack makes ChatGPT repeat a single token (e.g., "poem") indefinitely, causing generation to diverge and fall back to memorized pre-training data.
records.quote: In their attack, they make ChatGPT repeat a single token, expecting that the generation will diverge from the expected path. In the example provided in the paper, the authors make ChatGPT repeat the sequence “poem, poem, poem…” indefinitely. Even if the most probable token at each generation step is the word “poem”, nonzero probabilities are assigned to other tokens. Sampling repeatedly from the same distribution may cause the generator to output a low-probability token, thus diverging from the expected path. Once the generation diverges, ChatGPT seems to fall back to memorized data.

records.claim: Leaked data from the divergence attack comes from pre-training data, including personal, sensitive, and copyrighted material such as personal data, inappropriate content, book fragments, URLs, UUIDs, code snippets, research papers, and boilerplate texts.
records.quote: By comparing the behavior of gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-3.5-instruct-turbo, which are (presumably) fine-tuned on different data, the authors conclude that the leaked data comes from the data used during model pre-training, which likely includes personal, sensitive, and copyrighted material. Namely, the authors recover personal data, inappropriate content, fragments of books, URLs, UUIDs, code snippets, research papers, boilerplate texts, and mixed memorized data.

records.section: VIII-A Comparison of Different LLM-Enhanced RL Approaches

records.subject: Decision-Maker

records.subject: explainable AI systems

claims.claim: Explainable AI systems can fall prey to three main categories of attacks: integrity attacks, availability attacks, and privacy and confidentiality attacks.
claims.conditions: According to a classification system mentioned in (Biggio and Roli, 2018; Baniecki and Biecek, 2024)

records.quote: According to a classification system mentioned in ( Biggio and Roli, 2018 ; Baniecki and Biecek, 2024 ) , explainable AI systems can fall prey to three main categories of attacks: (i) integrity attacks, such as evasion and backdoor poisoning, leading to incorrect categorisation of certain data points ( Severi et al., 2021 ; Kuppa and Le-Khac, 2020 ; Liu et al., 2022c ; Nguyen et al., 2023b ) ; (ii) availability attacks, characterised by poisoning efforts aimed at inflating the error rate in classification tasks ( Abdukhamidov et al., 2023 ) ; and (iii) privacy and confidentiality attacks, aimed at extracting sensitive information from user data and the models themselves.

records.subject: Membership Inference Attacks (MIA)

claims.claim: Before model explanations, popular attacks are loss thresholding and likelihood ratio attack (LRT).
Loss thresholding identifies if a data point was in the training set by checking the model’s error rate against a threshold, requiring access to labels and model details.
claims.conditions: requiring access to labels and model details

claims.claim: LRT uses shadow models to compare confidence levels of data being in or out of the training set, calculating a likelihood ratio to predict membership without needing direct model access.

records.quote: Before model explanations, popular attacks are loss thresholding and likelihood ratio attack (LRT) ( Pawelczyk et al., 2023 ) . Loss thresholding identifies if a data point was in the training set by checking the model’s error rate against a threshold, requiring access to labels and model details ( Yeom et al., 2018 ; Sablayrolles et al., 2019 ) . LRT, in contrast, uses shadow models to compare confidence levels of data being in or out of the training set, calculating a likelihood ratio to predict membership without needing direct model access ( Carlini et al., 2022 ) .

records.subject: Threat model on gradient-based explanations

claims.claim: Most threat models are based on threshold-based attacks.
The reference/shadow model scenario assumes the attacker has some labeled data from the same distribution as the target model, as well as knowledge of the model’s architecture and hyperparameters.

records.quote: Most threat models are based on threshold-based attacks ( Shokri et al., 2021 ) . There are two key scenarios for this: the optimal threshold scenario, where the threshold is deduced from known data point memberships to gauge the maximum privacy risk; and the reference/shadow model scenario, which is more practical and assumes the attacker has some labeled data from the same distribution as the target model, as well as knowledge of the model’s architecture and hyperparameters in line with Kerckhoffs’s principle ( Petitcolas, 2023 ) .

records.subject: Differential Privacy

claims.claim: Differential privacy is a mathematically based privacy standard that defines privacy loss using a quantifiable metric.
It guarantees the aggregated data output will obscure the involvement of any individual record in the dataset.

records.quote: Differential privacy (DP) is a solid, mathematically based privacy standard that defines privacy loss using a quantifiable metric ( Liu et al., 2024c ) . It does so through mechanisms that guarantee the aggregated data output will obscure the involvement of any individual record in the dataset, as established by Dwork et al. ( Dwork et al., 2014 ) .

records.subject: Evaluation Metrics

claims.claim: Assess the range of attribute values within k-anonymous counterfactual instances. Consider all attributes, including those beyond quasi-identifiers
Assess equivalence classes within anonymized datasets, focusing on class label uniformity.

Reflect how often the model’s predictions are unchanged despite perturbations to the input, which would suggest that the explanation is effectively capturing the reasoning behind the model’s predictions.
A complete and faithful explanation to the model should inherently be sparse, focusing only on a select subset of features that are most predictive of the model’s decision.
Higher NCP values indicate a greater degree of generalization and more information loss. This metric helps in assessing the balance between data privacy and utility.
Measure the penalties on tuples in a dataset after k-anonymization, reflecting how indistinguishable they are post-anonymization
Measure the error caused by randomness added when minimizing the privacy loss as the expected deviation of the randomized explanation from the best local approximation
The higher the better but due to privacy-utility trade-off, this metric should not be 100%.
Refers to the number of individuals in the training dataset to whom a given explanation could potentially be linked

If an adversary can access model explanations, they would not gain any additional information that could help in inferring something about the training data beyond what could be learned from the model predictions alone
The explanation algorithm must not exceed the overall budget across all queries. Stricter requirement ( ε m i n , δ m i n ) is set for each individual query.
Evaluate an attack’s effectiveness in correctly and completely identifying the properties it is designed to infer.
Measures the accuracy of attack (e.g. membership prediction in membership inference attacks), on a balanced dataset of members and non-members.
An AUC near 1 indicates a highly successful privacy attack, while an AUC close to 0.5 suggests no better performance than random guessing.
If an attack can pinpoint even a minuscule fraction of the training dataset with high precision, then the attack ought to be deemed effective.
Gives an overview of how accurately an attack can reconstruct private inputs by averaging the absolute differences across all samples and features.
The ratio of successfully reconstructed features to the total number of features across all samples

A higher agreement indicates that the substitute model is more similar to the original model. When comparing two model extraction methods with the same agreement, the one with the lower standard deviation is preferred.
The degree to which a data reconstruction attack is accurate, measured by the reduction in uncertainty across all features of all samples in the dataset

records.subject: learning in SNN

claims.claim: Learning in SNN is divided into three categories: direct supervised learning, unsupervised learning (STDP), and indirect supervised learning (conversion of an ANN to SNN).

records.quote: The learning in SNN can be divided into three categories, i.e., (1) direct supervised learning (backpropagation-based etc.); (2) Unsupervised learning (spike timing-dependent plasticity – STDP); often, weights on the synapses are modified using the information locally available. This learning process is called local learning and it resembles the learning process in the neurons present in a human brain. (3) Indirect supervised learning (conversion of an ANN to SNN).

records.quote: In an early study, Weidinger et al. (2021) structured the LLM risk landscape into 6 broad areas (Figure 4 (b)). More recently, Mazeika et al. (2024) created a benchmark spanning 8 categories (Figure 4 (c)), and Vidgen et al. (2023) proposed a benchmark covering five harm areas based on severity and prevalence (Figure 4 (d)). While these approaches highlight critical and focused types of harm, they are not comprehensive, and their categories often overlap. Expanding on Weidinger et al. (2021) , Wang et al. (2023g) introduced a three-tier risk taxonomy with a more granular classification: 5 first-tier risk areas, 12 second-tier types, and 61 specific harm types.

records.subject: Language model attack strategies

claims.claim: Attack strategies are classified into four key areas: Completion Compliance, Instruction Indirection, Generalization Glide, and Model Manipulation.

records.quote: We classify attack strategies into four key areas: Completion Compliance , which arises from the pretraining stage and leverages the model’s text completion tendency through autoregressive generation; Instruction Indirection , using capabilities enabled by instruction tuning; Generalization Glide , reflecting the model’s capacity for generalization, including reasoning and multilingualism; and Model Manipulation , which indicates a customizable model achieved by directly changing parameters, activations, or configurations.

records.subject: Attack Strategies by Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Common strategies for jailbreak prompts exploit the inherent capabilities of language models.
Methods utilizing the completion tendency are described in Section 4.1.1.
Instruction tuning creates a vast space for attackers to compose attacks with newly unlocked abilities to elicit unsafe responses.
Generalizability enables language, ciphering, and domain transfer attacks.
Publishing LLM services or making weights/code available makes it possible to attack the model through model manipulation.

records.quote: It is these inherent capabilities of language models that common strategies for jailbreak prompts exploit (see Figure 6 ), as noted by Wei et al. (2023a) . Most generative language models are pretrained with autoregressive modeling , which endows them with the ability to “complete” passages based on previous context. This tendency is not always compatible with downstream tasks such as answering questions or chatting, and is often overridden by following training, but the foundation persists and can interfere with applications McCoy et al. (2023) . Methods that utilize this completion tendency are described in Section 4.1.1 . After pretraining, language models undergo instruction tuning to better adhere to diverse user requirements and constraints, including creative writing, code completion, and role-play, creating a vast space for attackers to compose attacks with these newly unlocked abilities, in order to elicit unsafe responses (Section 4.1.2 ) . Combined with various domains and languages of data that the model has ingested during the pretraining stage, the model also achieves generalizability that enables language, ciphering, and domain transfer attacks (Section 4.1.3 ) . Additionally, publishing LLM services or making LLM weights or code available makes it possible to attack the model through model manipulation , such as using uncommon decoding strategies or breaking the safety guardrails via fine-tuning on curated data (Section 4.1.4 ) .
records.section: 4.1 Attack Strategies by Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Model tuning is used to adapt pre-trained foundational models for specific use cases.

records.subject: epidemiological tasks

claims.claim: The work is categorized into four categories based on researchers’ goals: Detection, Surveillance, Prediction, and Projection.

records.quote: we provide a taxonomy from the perspective of epidemiologists and categorize the work we investigated into four categories based on researchers’ goals: Detection , Surveillance , Prediction , and Projection .

records.subject: detection tasks

claims.claim: Two different detection tasks are incorporated from the view of graph data: source detection and transmission detection.

records.quote: In this survey, we incorporate two different detection tasks from the view of graph data: source detection and transmission detection .

records.subject: Surveillance

claims.claim: Surveillance tasks aim at providing timely and accurate information to support decision-making and disease prevention.
real-time processing ability has been the most important requirement during modeling
claims.conditions: Since a prompt response is needed

records.subject: prediction tasks

claims.claim: Prediction tasks are classified into two categories based on the type of prediction target: Incidence Prediction and Trend Prediction.

records.quote: we further classify prediction tasks into two categories based on the type of prediction target: (1) Incidence Prediction. (2) Trend Prediction.

records.subject: Incidence Prediction

records.quote: The target of incidence prediction is to provide quantitative results. In epidemic forecasting, incidences can include the number of infections or deaths in the future

records.subject: Trend Prediction

records.quote: Different from incidence prediction task, which focuses on quantitative targets, the target of trend prediction tasks is to identify a higher-level epidemic spreading pattern.

records.quote: Most of the projection tasks we collected involve finding the optimal interventions or maximizing influence to achieve targets like curbing the spread of diseases.

records.subject: model outputs

claims.claim: Model outputs are summarized into three categories: scalar, graph, and action sequence.
Scalar outputs are usually used in prediction tasks which provide indicators of the epidemic like infected cases.
Works focusing on epidemic graph construction have model outputs that are graphs.
Projection tasks usually adopt Reinforcement Learning (RL), which outputs actions taken at each time step, forming a consecutive action sequence.

records.quote: In terms of model outputs, there are also three categories to summarize these works: scalar , graph , and action sequence . Scalar outputs are usually used in prediction tasks which provide indicators of the epidemic like infected cases. There are also some works that focus on epidemic graph construction and the outputs of their designed models are graphs   Shan et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 . Finally, the projection tasks we collected usually adopt Reinforcement Learning (RL), which outputs the actions taken at each time step, forming a consecutive action sequence   Jhun, 2021 ; Feng et al., 2023a ; Meirom et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2020 .

records.subject: Data Sources

claims.claim: Epidemic data can be accessed through public databases released by universities, governments, or other organizations, including demographic information like populations, number of infections, and health records.
Mobility information can be acquired through websites that record transportation information, maps, or contact records of individuals, usually used to construct the graph structure.

Epidemic information can be acquired through social media and online search records, where massive search of disease-related questions can indicate potential outbreaks and be utilized as node features.

Multi-modal data can be acquired through sensors like cameras, satellites, radios, etc., often requiring additional preprocessing using specialized models like ResNet before integration as node features.
Some research utilized simulated data for model training and testing, often requiring simulation models like TimeGEO, Independent Contagion Model (ICM), and SIR models to generate temporal graphs.

records.quote: We categorize these datasets based on their sources: (1) Demographic and Health Records. Epidemic data can be accessed through public databases released by universities, governments, or other organizations. These data usually include demographic information like populations, number of infections, and health records of individuals or groups. During epidemic graph construction, these data are usually used directly as node features or used in the construction of graph structures. (2) Mobility Information. Mobility information can be acquired through websites that record transportation information, maps, or contact records of individuals. This information is usually used to construct the graph structure. (3) Online Search and Social Media. Epidemic information can also be acquired through social media and online search records. The massive search of disease-related questions in a region can indicate potential outbreaks Lin et al., 2023 , which can then be utilized as node features. (4) Sensors. Multi-modal data can be acquired through sensors like cameras, satellites, radios, etc. These data can also help epidemic tasks like exposure risk prediction using images Han et al., 2023 . Unlike conventional data sources, sensor data often requires additional preprocessing using specialized models, such as encoding images with techniques like ResNet He et al., 2016 , before integration as node features. (5) Simulated Data. Besides real-world data, some research Tang et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Mežnar et al., 2021 also utilized simulated data for model training and testing. These data often require simulation models like TimeGEO Jiang et al., 2016 , Independent Contagion Model (ICM) Murphy et al., 2021 , and also SIR models to generate temporal graphs.

records.subject: graph construction

claims.claim: The taxonomy for graph construction is based on the dynamicity of nodes and edges.

records.quote: For graph construction, we provide a taxonomy based on the dynamicity of nodes and edges as follows.

records.subject: Static Node Features

claims.claim: Static node features refer to characteristics that do not change with time.
Most GNN tasks are using static features, except for tasks involving time series.

records.quote: Static node features typically refer to characteristics that do not change with time. ... Besides tasks involving time series, most GNN tasks are using static features.

records.subject: dynamic features

claims.claim: Dynamic features represent characteristics that change through time and are commonly seen in time-series forecasting tasks.
The shape of dynamic features can be represented as ℝ N × T × h, where T refers to the number of time points given.

records.quote: Contrary to static features, dynamic features represent characteristics that change through time. This type of data is commonly seen in time-series forecasting tasks and the models usually require inputs at each time point. Therefore, the shape of the dynamic features can be represented as ℝ N × T × h \mathbb{R}^{N\times T\times h} , where T T refers to the number of time points given.

records.subject: Static Graph Structure

claims.claim: Geographical adjacency is often employed to connect different regions represented as nodes in the graph.
The distance between regions or other features can be considered as the edge weights.
Another strategy focuses on exploring human mobility or transitions, e.g., linking nodes through nearest neighbors in the case of COVID-19 transmission.
In research where the node represents an individual, connections between two nodes often utilize contact information.
claims.conditions: where the node represents an individual

records.quote: The construction of a static graph structure typically entails the use of a predefined approach to generate the graph from available data. Once the graph is established, its structure remains unchanged throughout the training iterations or over different time points. For instance, in tasks involving multiple regions, the geographical adjacency A A , is often employed to connect different regions, which are represented as nodes in the graph G G   Pu et al., 2023a ; Yu et al., 2023a . The distance between regions or other features can be considered as the edge weights. Another strategy focuses on exploring human mobility or transitions, e.g . , linking nodes through nearest neighbors in the case of COVID-19 transmission. This method takes into consideration the distribution of the population and individual movements between various locations   Liu et al., 2023b ; Wang et al., 2023 . In research where the node represents an individual, connections between two nodes often utilize contact information, e.g . , identifying contacts at risk of spreading the disease as links between individuals   Gouareb et al., 2023a ; Tomy et al., 2022a .

records.subject: Dynamic Graph Structure

claims.claim: Determining the structure of a dynamic graph commonly involves one of two methodologies: modification of adjacency relations over time or learning of adaptive edges/weights during training.

records.quote: Determining the structure of a dynamic graph commonly involves one of two methodologies. One approach is the modification of adjacency relations over time or throughout the virus propagation process. ... Another strategy entails the learning of adaptive edges or edge weights during the training phase.

records.claim: Traditional geographical adjacency matrices fall short of accurately representing true connectivity, so recent studies aim for models to learn an adaptive relationship between nodes.
records.quote: Given the dynamic nature of disease transmission, which evolves at each time step, traditional geographical adjacency matrices fall short of accurately representing true connectivity. Recent studies Wang et al., 2022a ; Deng et al., 2020 ; Cao et al., 2022 have aimed for models to learn an adaptive relationship between nodes.

records.subject: GNNs in epidemic modeling

claims.claim: The methodologies are broadly classified into two categories: Neural Models and Hybrid Models.
Neural Models primarily focus on a data-driven approach and leverage deep learning to uncover complex patterns without explicit encoding of epidemiological processes.
Hybrid Models represent a synergistic fusion of mechanistic epidemiological models with neural networks.

records.quote: The methodologies of the GNNs in epidemic modeling can be broadly classified into two categories: Neural Models and Hybrid Models . ... (a) Neural Models primarily focus on a data-driven approach ... (b) On the other hand, Hybrid Models represent a synergistic fusion of mechanistic epidemiological models with neural networks.

records.subject: methods in epidemic modeling

claims.claim: Methods in epidemic modeling are divided into two categories: Neural Models and Hybrid Models.
Both Neural Models and Hybrid Models utilize GNNs as the backbone model.
Neural Models and Hybrid Models differ in the adoption of the mechanistic models.

records.quote: In this section, we provide a detailed illustration of the methods in epidemic modeling, which are divided into the two categories discussed in Section 3.4 : Neural Models and Hybrid Models . While both categories utilize GNNs as the backbone model as illustrated in Figure 3 , they differ in the adoption of the mechanistic models.

records.subject: Neural Models

claims.claim: Neural Models are GNN-based models that exclusively employ GNNs without incorporating mechanistic models.
claims.conditions: exclusively employed GNNs without incorporating mechanistic models

claims.claim: Neural Models are dissected through three perspectives: Spatial Dynamics Modeling, Temporal Dynamics Modeling, and Intervention Modeling.

records.quote: When utilizing GNNs for epidemic modeling, numerous studies have exclusively employed GNNs without incorporating mechanistic models into their tasks, which we term Neural Models. ... In this subsection, we delve into the (GNN-based) Neural Models in epidemic modeling, dissected through three perspectives: (a) Spatial Dynamics Modeling , (b) Temporal Dynamics Modeling , and (c) Intervention Modeling .

records.subject: GNNs in Epidemic Modeling
records.missing: Existing multi-scale models are limited to processing only two predefined scales, and there is a need for models capable of incorporating data across multiple dynamic scales.
records.quote: existing approaches are limited to processing only two predefined scales, such as county-level and state-level data. Looking ahead, there is growing anticipation for the development of novel models capable of incorporating data across multiple dynamic scales

records.subject: GNNs in Epidemic Modeling
records.missing: Current GNN methods are time-consuming for large-scale graphs (e.g., individual contact graphs in metropolises), especially when combined with multi-scale data and real-time processing requirements.
records.quote: the graph for individuals or other necessary parts in epidemic models can be extremely large, e.g., contact information graphs in metropolises, which could make the current methods very time-consuming.

records.subject: GNNs in Epidemic Modeling
records.missing: There has not been much work exploring the multi-modality of GNNs in an epidemiology setting, and existing works lack cross-modality in node features.
records.quote: there has not been much work exploring the multi-modality of GNNs in an epidemiology setting. Some related works Lin et al., 2023a ; Han et al., 2023 have utilized unstructured data like textual or image data to construct node features. However, there is no cross-modality in their work in terms of node features.

records.subject: GNNs in Epidemic Modeling
records.missing: Current GNN-based methods model disease spreading in a discrete manner, which is incompatible with the continuous nature of real-world disease spreading.
records.quote: All GNN-based methods discussed above involve information aggregation at one or several time points in a discrete manner. Nevertheless, in the real world, disease spreading is a continuous process, which is incompatible with current methods.

records.subject: GNNs in Epidemic Modeling
records.missing: Existing intervention modeling methods only include one type of intervention (node-level or edge-level), whereas real-world interventions happen at different graph levels and scales.
records.quote: However, each method only includes one type of intervention, either node-level or edge-level. In the real world, however, interventions can happen at different graph levels and also at different scales. To better model the real situation, multi-level and multi-scale interventions need to be introduced.

records.subject: Transformer-based networks as segmentation model architectures

claims.claim: TransUNet incorporates Transformer blocks as additional encoders to model bottleneck features.
UNETR employs the Transformer as the primary encoder path, combining it with a CNN decoder and skip connections to create a hybrid model.
DAE-Former integrates Transformers into dual attention blocks in both the encoder and decoder, enhancing the architecture with cross-attention in skip connections.
Swin UNETR features the Swin Transformer in the encoder section, complemented by a CNN-based decoder and skip connections to form a hybrid model.
TransFuse fuses the Transformer and CNN encoder to connect the decoder.
nnFormer incorporates Transformers in both the encoder and decoder for its architecture.

records.quote: (a) TransUNet Chen et al (2021) incorporates Transformer blocks as additional encoders to model bottleneck features. (b) UNETR Hatamizadeh et al (2022) employs the Transformer as the primary encoder path, combining it with a CNN decoder and skip connections to create a hybrid model. (c) DAE-Former Azad et al (2023) integrates Transformers into dual attention blocks in both the encoder and decoder, enhancing the architecture with cross-attention in skip connections. (d) Swin UNETR Hatamizadeh et al (2021) features the Swin Transformer in the encoder section, complemented by a CNN-based decoder and skip connections to form a hybrid model. (e) TransFuse Zhang et al (2021) fuses the Transformer and CNN encoder to connect the decoder. (f) nnFormer Zhou et al (2021) incorporates Transformers in both the encoder and decoder for its architecture.

records.subject: 3D Egocentric Pose Estimation Methods

claims.claim: Methods are classified into two categories: skeletal and body shape based approaches.
Skeletal-based methods leverage human skeleton representation to track and infer 3D joint position and body movements.
Body shape based methods utilize a parametric model, such as SMPL and SMPL-X, to estimate 3D joint locations and body shapes.
claims.claims_about: Human body shape based human body pose estimation methods

records.quote: we discuss around 35 popular techniques by classifying them into two categories, namely skeletal and body shape based approaches. Skeletal-based 3D pose estimation methods [ 49 , 56 , 57 ] leverage the human skeleton representation to accurately track and infer 3D joint position and body movements. Human body shape based human body pose estimation methods [ 8 , 73 , 23 ] utilize a parametric model, such as SMPL [ 41 ] and SMPL-X [ 50 ] , to accurately estimate 3D joint locations and body shapes.

records.subject: Group fairness

records.subject: Demographic Parity

claims.claim: Demographic parity ensures that the predicted outcome Y ^ \hat{Y} of an ML model is independent of sensitive attribute S S

records.quote: Demographic parity ensures that the predicted outcome Y ^ \hat{Y} of an ML model is independent of sensitive attribute S S ( Grari et al., 2020 ) .

records.subject: Conditional Statistical Parity

claims.claim: Conditional statistical parity, also known as conditional demographic parity, requires the outcome for different sensitive groups to be the same, even after adding extra features

records.quote: Conditional statistical parity, also known as conditional demographic parity, requires the outcome for different sensitive groups to be the same, even after adding extra features ( Corbett-Davies et al., 2017 ) .

records.subject: Individual fairness

claims.claim: Fairness through awareness and fairness through unawareness both fall under the umbrella of individual fairness.
claims.conditions: because they are related to how individuals are treated by the ML model on a one-to-one basis

records.subject: Fairness through Unawareness

records.subject: Data-Driven Bias

records.quote: This section describes biases that arise in the outcomes of models that learn patterns from the training data.

records.subject: Measurement Bias

claims.claim: Measurement bias is introduced when subjective choices are made for the model design.

records.quote: Measurement bias is introduced when subjective choices are made for the model design ( Fahse et al., 2021 ) .

records.subject: Representation Bias

claims.claim: Representation bias can occur during the data collection or sampling phase when the probability distribution of the training samples is not the same as the true underlying distribution.

records.quote: Representation bias can occur during the data collection or sampling phase when the probability distribution of the training samples is not the same as the true underlying distribution ( Fahse et al., 2021 ) .

records.subject: Label Bias

claims.claim: Label bias or annotation bias arises when labels used to train the model are not entirely correct.

records.quote: Label bias or annotation bias arises when labels used to train the model are not entirely correct.

records.subject: Co-variate Shift

claims.claim: This kind of bias arises when the distribution of the features used to train the model is different in the training and testing phase.

records.quote: This kind of bias arises when the distribution of the features used to train the model is different in the training and testing phase.

records.subject: Sampling Bias

claims.claim: Sampling bias can occur when sampling of subgroups is not random.

records.quote: Sampling bias can occur when sampling of subgroups is not random ( Mehrabi et al., 2021 ) .

records.subject: Specification Bias

claims.claim: This sort of bias arises during the specification of what comprises the input and output during a learning task.

records.quote: This sort of bias arises during the specification of what comprises the input and output during a learning task ( Hellström et al., 2020 ) .

records.subject: Aggregation Bias

claims.claim: This bias arises when the true underlying patterns are misinterpreted by how the data is combined.

records.quote: This bias arises when the true underlying patterns are misinterpreted by how the data is combined.

records.subject: Linking Bias

claims.claim: Linking bias occurs when true behavior of users is misrepresented due to the attributes of networks derived from user interactions, connections or activity.

records.quote: Linking bias occurs when true behavior of users is misrepresented due to the attributes of networks derived from user interactions, connections or activity ( Olteanu et al., 2019 ) .

records.subject: Inherited Bias

claims.claim: Inherited bias arises when biased output from a tool is used as input for other machine learning algorithms.

records.quote: According to ( Hellström et al., 2020 ) inherited bias arises when biased output from a tool is used as input for other machine learning algorithms.

records.subject: Longitudinal Data Fallacy

claims.claim: This sort of bias can arise when cross-sectional analysis is performed to study temporal data.

records.quote: This sort of bias can arise when cross-sectional analysis is performed to study temporal data.
